senses.definition: A large amount.
senses.example: I have a lot of things to say.

senses.definition: Many things, much.
senses.example: A lot depends on whether your parents agree.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see a,‎ lot.
senses.example: A lot of tourists has left the hotel already, but there's another good lot that still remains there.

senses.definition: Very much; a great deal; to a large extent.
senses.example: Thanks a lot for listening to me.

senses.definition: Often; frequently.
senses.example: I go swimming a lot.

senses.definition: Difficult to handle emotionally.
senses.example: Yeah, it's a lot.

senses.definition: Too much, busy.
senses.example: This week has been a lot, with three deadlines and two outages.

senses.definition: Dramatic, extra.
senses.example: Honestly, your reaction to the spilled coffee was a lot, even for you.

core.definition: A large amount or number; or to a great extent or degree. Used alone or with 'of' before a noun, as in 'I like it a lot'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'lot', and the vowel is an open 'ah' sound, the same vowel many Americans use in 'cot' and 'caught'. The 't' is often flapped or dropped in fast speech, so it sounds like 'uh LAH-duh' or 'uh LAH'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it expresses a generous amount, but it can sound vague in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'a lot' constantly in speech, as in 'Thanks a lot' or 'I like it a lot.' It is informal in writing, so in reports or academic work use 'a great deal', 'much', or 'considerably'. Often 'a lot' is written incorrectly as 'alot', which is not standard.

distinctions.note: 'Much' is common in questions and negatives, as in 'not much', while 'a lot' is more natural in positive statements.
'A great deal' is slightly more formal and thoughtful, while 'a lot' is everyday speech.
'Lots' is even more casual and common in speech, as in 'lots of fun' or 'I like it lots'.

examples.everyday: Thanks a lot for picking up the kids today, I really appreciate it.
examples.professional: The new dashboard saves our team a lot of time every week, so I think we should keep it.
examples.analytical: The argument depends a lot on how we define fairness, and the author never makes that definition clear.

nuance.analogy: Like a full pantry: there is plenty to go around, so you don't need to count every item.
nuance.etymology: 'Lot' comes from Old English 'hlot', meaning a share or portion, so 'a lot' originally meant a large share.
common_mistakes: Writing 'alot' as one word, which is not standard in American writing.
Forgetting 'of' before a noun, as in 'a lot people'; say 'a lot of people' instead.

senses.definition: Embarrassed, disconcerted, or ashamed.

core.definition: Embarrassed or ashamed, especially after being noticed, corrected or praised in a way that makes you feel awkward.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BASH, with a short a as in 'cat'. The -ed ending is just a final t sound, not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It describes a quiet, self-conscious embarrassment and usually sounds gentle rather than harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use abashed mostly in writing and in slightly formal or literary speech. In everyday talk they usually say 'embarrassed' or 'sheepish'. A natural reply to someone who says you look abashed is a laugh and a casual 'Yeah, I know'.

distinctions.note: Embarrassed is the common everyday word and can describe a small, brief moment. Abashed is more formal and suggests a deeper sense of being put in a lower position.
Ashamed implies you have done something wrong and feel guilty. Abashed can describe embarrassment without any real wrongdoing.

examples.everyday: I felt abashed when I forgot my neighbor's name right after she introduced herself.
examples.professional: The new engineer looked abashed when the senior analyst pointed out the bug in his pull request.
examples.analytical: Shame turns a person inward, while the abashed person is often caught between wanting to hide and wanting to be seen correctly.

nuance.analogy: Like a student who raises a hand with a wrong answer and feels the room turn toward them: a small, sudden heat in the face.
nuance.etymology: From Old French esbahir, meaning to be astonished, from es- and bahir, to gape in astonishment.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable 'uh-BASH-id'; it is one syllable ending in t.
Using abashed for a very serious shame; it is too mild for serious wrongdoing.
Writing 'abashed about' when a preposition is needed; 'abashed at' or 'abashed by' are more standard.

senses.definition: Differing from the norm.
senses.example: The lab results were aberrant, so we reran the model with cleaner data.

senses.definition: Straying from the right way; deviating from morality or truth.
senses.example: Her aberrant conduct led the elders to question her commitment to the community's values.

senses.definition: Deviating from the ordinary or natural type; exceptional; abnormal.
senses.example: Weather patterns over the Midwest have been aberrant this spring, with unusually heavy rain.

senses.definition: A person or object that deviates from the rest of a group.
senses.example: The researchers discarded the aberrant from the sample because its readings were far outside the cluster.

senses.definition: A group, individual, or structure that deviates from the usual or natural type, especially with an atypical chromosome number.
senses.example: The geneticist reported that the aberrant carried an extra copy of chromosome 21.

core.definition: Departing from what is normal, typical, or expected, often in a way that seems unacceptable or surprising.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the first vowel is the weak uh sound. Many learners say AB-er-ant, which shifts the stress to the wrong place for the adjective.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral; it signals a departure from what should be expected, but in science it can be a neutral technical label.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aberrant in scientific reports, medical writing, and formal criticism, such as 'aberrant behavior' or 'aberrant results.' In casual conversation, people would say weird, off, or unusual. Calling a person aberrant can sound harsh, so use it carefully about people.

distinctions.note: Abnormal is the common everyday word for something outside the average, while aberrant implies a clear departure from an expected pattern or standard.
Deviant carries strong social or moral judgment, whereas aberrant is more clinical and neutral about the reason for the departure.
Eccentric describes a harmless quirk in a person's style, while aberrant describes behavior or results that break a pattern.

examples.everyday: The car made a weird noise this morning, which is aberrant for a new engine, so I took it to the shop.
examples.professional: Several data points in the July report look aberrant, so let's exclude them before we retrain the model.
examples.analytical: Durkheim treated aberrant behavior not as pure individual failure but as a symptom of breakdowns in the social order.

nuance.analogy: Like one note in a song that falls outside the key: the melody is normal, but that one note stands out sharply.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aberrans, present participle of aberrare, 'to wander away,' from ab- 'away' plus errare 'to wander.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AB-er-ant, which is a common error for this adjective.
Using aberrant for simple surprises, such as a late bus, where weird or unusual is more natural.

aberrant.etymology: From Latin *aberrāns*, present active participle of *aberrō* (“go astray; err”), from *ab* (“from”) + *errō* (“to wander”).

core.definition: A priest of Israel, son of Ahimelech, who fled with David and served as high priest until Solomon removed him.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BY. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the -thar ending has a strong American r and an open ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In Scripture he is a mixed figure: loyal to David early on, but later removed from the priesthood.
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name, used in Bible study, church and sermons when discussing David's reign and the succession to Solomon. Americans rarely meet it outside Scripture. Its three syllables are pronounced clearly in reading.

examples.everyday: Do you remember Abiathar from the stories about David? He was the priest who escaped the massacre at Nob.
examples.professional: In the Old Testament survey, Abiathar is useful for explaining the shift in priestly leadership from Eli's line to Zadok.
examples.analytical: 1 Kings 2:26-27 narrates Solomon's removal of Abiathar from the priesthood, and many readers see this as the fulfillment of an earlier prophecy against the house of Eli.

nuance.analogy: Like a loyal official who served under one ruler and was dismissed when the throne changed hands.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Evyatar, probably meaning father of abundance or my father is excellent.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Confusing Abiathar with Abimelech or Ahimelech, other priestly names in Samuel.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, Abiathar is Evyatar, probably meaning father of abundance. He is the son of Ahimelech the priest, and the only one of his family who escaped Saul's massacre at Nob, fleeing to David with the ephod (1 Samuel 22:20-23). He carried the ark with Zadok during Absalom's rebellion, but David sent them back to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:24-29). Solomon later removed him from the priesthood and sent him to Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26-27).

senses.definition: In an abstracted manner; separately; in the abstract.
senses.example: She listened abstractedly while her son described his soccer game, nodding now and then.

senses.definition: With absence of mind.

core.definition: In a distracted or absent-minded way, as if thinking about something else and not paying attention to what's around you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRAK. Say the first syllable as a weak 'uh' and don't reduce the -ly ending to nothing; it is a clear 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a preoccupied manner without judging it harshly.
nuance.usage_note: This is a formal adverb you will mostly see in novels, reviews, or written descriptions of behavior. Americans in conversation would say 'absentmindedly' or 'like she wasn't really there.' Use it to describe actions that look distracted.

distinctions.note: Absentmindedly is more common in everyday American speech and often implies forgetfulness; abstractedly emphasizes deep thought.

examples.everyday: She nodded abstractedly when I asked if she wanted coffee, so I'm not sure she heard me.
examples.professional: He answered the question abstractedly while scrolling through his email, so I repeated it in writing.
examples.analytical: The narrator wanders abstractedly through the city, his mind turning over a problem he cannot yet name.

nuance.analogy: Like someone turning the pages of a magazine while their thoughts are miles away.
nuance.etymology: From abstracted (from Latin abstrahere, 'to draw away') plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it when you mean 'in the abstract' or theoretically; in the everyday sense it describes a distracted manner.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress falls on STRAK, the second syllable of the word, so say ub-STRAK-tid-lee.

senses.definition: Designating a line of verse having the required number of syllables in the last foot.
A verse which has the complete number of feet and syllables.
senses.example: The poem's opening line is acatalectic, so it has exactly the full number of syllables.

core.definition: Of a line of verse: complete, having the full number of syllables in its final foot, with no syllable missing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEK, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable, ay. Do not stress the -cat- syllable, and say the final -tik with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term from prosody with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist word from poetry and metrics, used in literary criticism, poetry classes and scholarly writing about meter. Americans almost never use it in conversation. In ordinary speech, say that a line is 'complete' or 'has all its syllables'.

distinctions.note: A catalectic line is missing a syllable in its final foot, while an acatalectic line is complete. The two words are opposites in metrical analysis.

examples.professional: The editor flagged the final stanza as acatalectic, so we should double-check the meter before the book goes to print.
examples.analytical: Because the closing lines are acatalectic, the poem ends with a full, settled beat rather than trailing off into silence.

nuance.analogy: Like a sentence that ends exactly where it should, with no word cut short.
nuance.etymology: From Greek akatalēktos 'not left incomplete', from a- 'not' plus katalēgein 'to stop short'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with catalectic, which means the opposite (a missing final syllable).
Stressing the first syllable, ay, instead of LEK.

acatalectic.etymology: From Late Latin *acatalēcticus*, from Ancient Greek *ἀκατάληκτος* (“leaving off”).

senses.definition: In an accidental manner; by chance, unexpectedly.
senses.example: He discovered penicillin largely accidentally.

senses.definition: Unintentionally.
senses.example: He accidentally exposed the bacteria to mold spores.

senses.definition: Used with the verb omitted but implied, the verb itself having the meaning 'omit', 'delete' or similar.
senses.example: I accidentally the word 'not'. (meaning "I accidentally omitted the word 'not'")

core.definition: By chance, or without meaning to do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DENT, and the unstressed -ent-ally is reduced to 'uh-lee', often said quickly. The word has four syllables, so do not drop the middle syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common word for apologies and explanations, and can be reassuring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use accidentally constantly in everyday speech, especially to apologize or explain: 'I accidentally deleted your file.' It usually comes before the main verb. 'By accident' is also common, as in 'I found it by accident.' A common American joke is 'accidentally on purpose', used when someone seems to have caused something deliberately.

distinctions.note: Unintentionally is more formal and is common in written apologies and reports, while accidentally is the everyday choice in speech.
Incidentally means 'by the way' or as a side point, so do not use it when you mean by chance.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I accidentally hung up on you when you were still talking.
examples.professional: I accidentally sent the draft to the whole team, so please ignore that email.
examples.analytical: The discovery was accidentally made, yet it reshaped the methods of the entire field.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone skipping across water when you never aimed for it.
nuance.etymology: From accident, from Latin accidere, to happen, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as accidently; the correct spelling has the -ally ending.
Using incidentally to mean by chance; incidentally means 'by the way'.

senses.definition: Sloth, slothfulness, especially as inducing general listlessness and apathy.

core.definition: Spiritual sloth: a listless weariness or apathy that drains your energy and interest in duties, prayer and ordinary life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AK. The cc is pronounced /ks/, and the ending is a clear 'dee', not 'dy'. The unstressed middle syllable is a weak 'suh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a moral or spiritual failing, not ordinary tiredness, and sounds heavy in use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in theology, church history or literature, usually when discussing the medieval list of deadly sins. In daily speech people say 'I'm in a funk' or 'I can't get motivated' instead. Using it in casual conversation may sound pretentious unless the topic is religious or philosophical.

distinctions.note: Sloth is the general word for laziness; accidie is the more specific spiritual weariness that makes prayer and duty feel pointless.
Apathy is simply not caring; accidie often includes restlessness and sadness, not just indifference.
Acedia is the Latin and Greek form used by theologians; accidie is the Middle English spelling, and both mean the same thing.

examples.everyday: I've had a bad case of accidie all week; I can't make myself answer any texts.
examples.professional: After the third failed launch, the whole team slipped into a quiet accidie that nobody wanted to name in standup.
examples.analytical: Evagrius describes accidie as the noonday demon that makes the monk keep staring at the sun and longing for the day to end.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone battery that charges to full but drains in minutes, leaving you unable to start anything.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin accidia, from Greek akēdia, 'lack of care', from a- 'without' and kēdos 'care'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'accident' or 'accidentally'; the words are unrelated.
Using it for ordinary tiredness; it implies a deeper spiritual or moral weariness.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

accidie.etymology: From Middle English *accidie*, from Anglo-Norman *accidie*, Old French *accide*, *accidie*, from Late Latin *accīdia*, alteration of *acēdia* (“sloth, torpor”), from Ancient Greek *ἀκήδεια* (“indifference”), from *ἀ-* + *κῆδος*.

senses.definition: To render fit, suitable, or correspondent; to adapt.
senses.example: to accommodate ourselves to circumstances

senses.definition: To cause to come to agreement; to bring about harmony; to reconcile.
senses.example: to accommodate differences

senses.definition: To provide with something desired, needed, or convenient.
senses.example: to accommodate a friend with a loan

senses.definition: To provide housing for.
senses.example: to accommodate an old friend for a week

senses.definition: To provide sufficient space for.
To contain comfortably; to have space for.
senses.example: This venue accommodates three hundred people.

senses.definition: To do a favor or service for; to oblige.
senses.example: Could you accommodate me by moving our meeting to Thursday afternoon?

senses.definition: To give consideration to; to allow for.
senses.example: The new budget can accommodate the extra staff without cutting any programs.

senses.definition: To show the correspondence of; to apply or make suit by analogy; to adapt or fit, as teachings to accidental circumstances, statements to facts, etc.
senses.example: to accommodate prophecy to events

senses.definition: Of an eye, to change focal length in order to focus at a different distance.
senses.example: The optometrist explained how the eye can accommodate quickly when focusing on a nearby book.

senses.definition: (rare) To adapt oneself; to be conformable or adapted; become adjusted.
senses.example: She just needed some time to accommodate to the situation.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To provide space, lodging, or what someone needs, or to adjust your plans to suit other people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAH, which uses the 'cot' vowel in General American. The middle syllables are reduced, and the final -ate is 'ayt.' Do not use an 'aw' vowel or say uh-kom-uh-DAYT.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals helpfulness and flexibility, but in very casual speech it can sound stiff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use accommodate in polite service and business language, such as 'Can you accommodate a party of six?' or 'We can accommodate your schedule.' In casual speech 'make room for' or 'fit in' is more common. Use it for hotels, restaurants, events, and reasonable requests.

distinctions.note: Both begin with ac-, but accompany means to go along with someone, while accommodate means to provide for needs or make room.
Adapt means changing yourself or something to fit a situation; accommodate often means making room for someone else's needs.

examples.everyday: The restaurant can accommodate a group of eight if you call ahead.
examples.professional: Can we accommodate the client's deadline by moving the sprint review to Friday?
examples.analytical: A good moral theory must accommodate our considered intuitions about cases without simply bending to them.

nuance.analogy: Like a flexible seat in a crowded car that shifts to fit one more passenger.
nuance.etymology: From Latin accommodare, to fit to or adapt, from ad- 'to' and commodus, suitable.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with one c or one m; it has two c's and two m's.
Using it for vague help in casual speech, where 'help out' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: In English and other modern languages, the case used to mark the immediate object (direct object) on which the transitive verb acts. In Latin grammar, the accusative case (cāsus accūsātīvus) includes functions derived from the Indo-European accusative and lative cases; said Lative Case expresses concepts similar to those of the English prepositions "to" and "towards".
senses.example: In German, the accusative case marks the direct object, as in 'Ich sehe den Mann.'

core.definition: In English and other languages, the grammatical case marking a noun or pronoun as the direct object of a transitive verb or the object of certain prepositions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on case in this phrase, while accusative itself is stressed on -KYOO- when said alone. The final -ive is a short unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical grammatical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use accusative case mainly in linguistics, Latin, German, and grammar teaching. In everyday English people say object pronoun, and they might say me or him is the object form. The term is common in language courses and grammar books, but it sounds academic in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Objective case is the common English term for object pronouns like me, him, and her, while accusative is the broader term used in many languages and in comparative grammar.
The nominative case marks the subject of a verb, while the accusative marks the direct object.
The dative case marks the indirect object or recipient, while the accusative marks the direct object that the action falls on.

examples.everyday: My daughter is learning German, and her teacher keeps saying that den is the accusative form for masculine nouns.
examples.professional: The documentation is clear that the accusative case marks the direct object in these parser rules.
examples.analytical: In English the accusative survives only in pronouns such as me, him, and them, so the case system is largely fossilized compared with Latin.

nuance.analogy: The accusative case is like a label on a package showing what the action lands on, marking the receiver of the verb's force.
nuance.etymology: From Latin accusativus, a mistranslation of Greek aitiatikē ptōsis 'causal case', from aitia 'cause', with the sense shifted through Latin accusare 'to accuse'.
common_mistakes: Confusing accusative with accuse, since the word looks like a verb form but names a grammatical case.
Assuming English has many accusative nouns; in English the accusative appears mainly in pronouns like me and him.

core.definition: A woman in Genesis, wife of Lamech and mother of Jabal and Jubal; a different Adah is also named as a wife of Esau.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the last vowel to a soft uh. Many Americans say AY-duh, like the name Ada, so both are heard, but the stress stays on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a biblical name that sounds natural in religious settings.
nuance.usage_note: Adah comes up mostly in Bible study, sermons and discussions of Genesis, not in everyday conversation. Americans hear it as a personal name, so in a conversation you should add context such as the Bible or Genesis to make clear which Adah you mean.

examples.everyday: At Bible study last night, someone asked about Adah, and nobody could remember who she was.
examples.professional: In the lesson on Lamech's family, I'll point out Adah and her sons Jabal and Jubal.
examples.analytical: Genesis 4:19 names Adah and Zillah as Lamech's two wives, which invites reflection on the Cainite line and its culture.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʿĀdâ, commonly rendered 'adornment' or 'ornament'; the exact root is debated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ah-DUH) instead of the first.
Confusing Adah with Ada or Adam when writing lists of Bible names.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ʿĀdâ, commonly rendered 'adornment'. Genesis 4:19-22 names Adah as Lamech's wife and the mother of Jabal, the ancestor of those who dwell in tents with livestock, and of Jubal, the ancestor of those who play the lyre and pipe. Genesis 4:23 records Lamech's address to Adah and Zillah. Genesis 36:2 names an Adah as a wife of Esau, so the name appears in more than one family line.

senses.definition: A person descended from the biblical Adam.
(historical) A member of one of a number of sects which professed to worship God in the same way that Adam did.
senses.example: Historians describe the Adamite sects as small groups that rejected clothing as a form of innocence.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the Biblical Adam.
senses.example: Adamite language

core.definition: A descendant of the biblical Adam, meaning any human being, or a member of a historical sect claiming Adam's innocence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AD. The first vowel is short, as in Adam, and the ending -ite is pronounced like 'myte'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a technical or historical term, though it can sound quaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use Adamite. You will meet it in theology, church history or older writing. In everyday speech, people say human, people or humankind. Be careful to distinguish the general meaning from the name of a historical sect.

distinctions.note: Adamic is the adjective meaning relating to Adam; Adamite is the noun for a descendant of Adam or a sect member.
Human being is the everyday phrase; Adamite is rare and emphasizes common descent from the biblical Adam.

examples.everyday: Grandpa liked to joke that we're all Adamites, so nobody gets out of doing the dishes.
examples.professional: In the church history class, we read about Adamite groups that claimed to recover Adam's innocence.
examples.analytical: Medieval groups that called themselves Adamites sought a return to a state before the fall, which the church treated as heresy.

nuance.analogy: Like a name for everyone in the same family tree, all traced back to one ancestor.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin Adamita, from Hebrew 'adam', meaning man or humankind.
common_mistakes: Using Adamite as an everyday synonym for person; in ordinary speech, say person or human.
Confusing the noun Adamite with the adjective Adamic.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'adam means man or humankind, and in Genesis the name Adam first refers to the first man. Genesis 5:1-2 introduces the book of the generations of Adam and says that God created humankind male and female. 1 Corinthians 15:45-49 calls Adam the first man and contrasts him with Christ as the last Adam.

senses.definition: Sticky; tenacious, as glutinous substances.
senses.example: adhesive material

senses.definition: Apt or tending to adhere; clinging.
senses.example: The adhesive quality of the wet clay made it hard to pull the mold apart cleanly.

senses.definition: A substance, such as glue, that provides or promotes adhesion.
senses.example: The label wouldn’t stick without strong adhesive.

core.definition: A substance, such as glue or tape, that makes two surfaces stick together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, HEE, and the first vowel is reduced. The final -ive is a short 'iv', not 'eve'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a product or material without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adhesive as a noun for glue-like products, and as an adjective in phrases such as self-adhesive label or adhesive tape. In casual talk, people say glue, tape or sticky stuff. Adhesive is more precise in packaging, hardware and construction contexts.

distinctions.note: Glue is the everyday word for a sticky substance, while adhesive is broader and more technical, covering tapes and films too.
Sticky describes a surface in plain language, while adhesive is more precise in product and technical contexts.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the adhesive tape? The box keeps coming open.
examples.professional: We switched to a water-based adhesive, which lowers emissions on the assembly line.
examples.analytical: The adhesive properties of the film depend on surface energy as much as on its chemical composition.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note: it holds only where you press it against a surface.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin adhaesivus, from adhaerere 'to stick to'.
common_mistakes: Using adhesive as a verb; the verb is adhere.
Saying adhesive for the whole concept of sticking; for that, use adhesion in formal writing.

adhesive.etymology: From French *adhésif*, from Medieval Latin *adhaesivus*, from *adhaereō* (supine *adhaesum*); see *adhere*.

senses.definition: Said to wish a final farewell; goodbye.
A farewell, a goodbye; especially a fond farewell, or a lasting or permanent farewell.
senses.example: We bid our final adieus to our family, then boarded the ship, bound for America.

core.definition: A formal or literary word for goodbye, especially a final or long parting, or a fond farewell.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final vowel is a long oo sound, not the yoo sound used in British English. The first vowel is a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly elegant; it signals a serious or sentimental farewell and can sound theatrical if used casually.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use adieu in everyday talk; they say bye, goodbye or see you later. You will hear it in literature, speeches, toasts or a dramatic farewell, and it can sound old-fashioned or showy in casual conversation. A natural reply is simply adieu or take care.

distinctions.note: Goodbye is the everyday, neutral word for any parting, while adieu is formal and often suggests a long or final separation.
Farewell is common in speeches, ceremonies and announcements, and it works as both a noun and an interjection; adieu is more literary and less common in ordinary American speech.

examples.everyday: We said our adieus at the airport, and I think we both teared up a little.
examples.professional: Please join me in a fond adieu to Maria, who retires after twenty-five years on our team.
examples.analytical: Many modern elegies read as a long adieu to the certainties of the old faith rather than a simple rejection of it.

nuance.analogy: Like a formal bow at the end of a play, rather than a casual wave from the car window.
nuance.etymology: From Old French a Dieu, literally 'to God', as in commending someone into God's care.
common_mistakes: Using adieu for a quick goodbye at a store or in an email; in those situations bye or take care is natural.
Pronouncing the final sound as yoo, as in British English; American speakers use oo.

adieu.etymology: From Middle English *adieu* also *adew*, *adewe*, *adue*, from Old French *adieu* (“to God”), a shortening of *a Dieu vous comant* (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin *ad Deum* (“to God”).

senses.definition: To postpone.
senses.example: The trial was adjourned for a week.

senses.definition: To defer; to put off temporarily or indefinitely.
senses.example: The judge adjourned the hearing until Monday so the lawyers could review the new evidence.

senses.definition: To end or suspend an event.
senses.example: The court will adjourn for lunch.

senses.definition: (uncommon) To move as a group from one place to another.
senses.example: After the dinner, we will adjourn to the bar.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To stop a meeting or court session and resume it later, or to end a gathering for a while.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is a strong rhotic ER sound. The final n is clearly pronounced, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a formal, procedural word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adjourn mainly for meetings, court sessions and legislatures. At work someone might say let's adjourn for lunch or the meeting is adjourned. In casual talk people say wrap up, end, or break for lunch.

distinctions.note: Postpone means delay an event to a later date; adjourn usually means stop a session and continue it later.
A recess is a short break within a session; adjourn ends the session until a set time.

examples.everyday: Okay, it's almost noon, so let's adjourn and grab lunch.
examples.professional: The chair asked for a motion to adjourn after we finished the budget items.
examples.analytical: The tribunal adjourned the hearing indefinitely, leaving the question of jurisdiction unresolved.

nuance.analogy: Adjourning a meeting is like pausing a movie: the story stops, and you pick it up later.
nuance.etymology: From Old French ajorner, to set a day for a meeting, from Latin ad diurnum, to a day.
common_mistakes: Using adjourn for simply leaving a party; it is for formal meetings and sessions.
Saying adjourn to mean end forever; it usually means stop now and continue later.

adjourn.etymology: From Middle English *ajournen*, from Old French *ajorner* (French *ajourner*), from the phrase *a* *jor* (*nomer*) ("to an day").

senses.definition: An appendage; something attached to something else in a subordinate capacity.
senses.example: The new lab was an adjunct to the main hospital, linked by a covered walkway.

senses.definition: A person associated with another, usually in a subordinate position; a colleague.
senses.example: She joined the research group as an adjunct, working under the senior investigator.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of adjunct professor.
An unmalted grain or grain product that supplements the main mash ingredient.
senses.example: Brewers often use rice as an adjunct to lighten the body of a lager.

senses.definition: A phrase within a clause or sentence that is grammatically dispensable but not semantically so, modifying the meaning.
senses.example: In the sentence, the prepositional phrase acts as an adjunct, modifying when the event occurred.

senses.definition: A graphic element that modifies another, such as (in Linear B script) a small syllabogram that is attached to a logogram as an abbreviation of an adjective that modifies that logogram (rather than as a phonetic complement that disambiguates the logogram).
senses.example: In Linear B tablets, a small syllabogram often serves as an adjunct attached to a logogram.

senses.definition: A constituent which is both the daughter and the sister of an X-bar.
senses.example: In this X-bar structure, the adjunct sits between the intermediate and maximal projections.

senses.definition: Symploce.
senses.example: The adjunct in the sermon repeated the same words at both the start and end of each line.

senses.definition: One of a pair of morphisms which relate to each other through a pair of adjoint functors.
senses.example: Each adjunct in the pair determines the other, so the two morphisms are closely related.

senses.definition: A key or scale closely related to another as principal; a relative or attendant key.
senses.example: A-minor is the adjunct key to C major, since they share the same notes.

senses.definition: (dated) A quality or property of the body or mind, whether natural or acquired, such as color in the body or judgment in the mind.
senses.example: In that old treatise, judgment was described as a mental adjunct, as natural as complexion.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Connected in a subordinate function.
senses.example: The adjunct role of the assistant secretary is subordinate to the director's authority.

senses.definition: Added to a faculty or staff in a secondary position.
senses.example: The university added two adjunct instructors to the writing staff this fall.

senses.definition: To work as an adjunct professor.
senses.example: After retiring from the bank, he adjuncted at the community college for several years.

core.definition: Something attached to a main thing in a secondary role; also a part-time teacher hired on a course-by-course basis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AD. The middle vowel is a short uh, and the ngkt ending is one syllable, so do not insert an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use; in academia the word can carry a hint of precarious, underpaid work.
nuance.usage_note: Adjunct is common at American universities, where an adjunct professor is a part-time instructor, often paid per course and without tenure. In everyday talk people say part-time teacher or instructor. In grammar, adjunct is a technical term for an optional phrase that adds detail.

distinctions.note: An associate professor is a full-time, usually tenured faculty rank; an adjunct is typically part-time and temporary.
Accessory is a general word for an extra item; adjunct is more formal and often refers to a role or position.

examples.everyday: My neighbor teaches as an adjunct at the community college and works two other jobs too.
examples.professional: We hired two adjunct instructors to cover the extra sections of statistics this fall.
examples.analytical: The author treats ethical reflection as an adjunct to scientific method rather than its foundation.

nuance.analogy: An adjunct is like a side room added to a house: useful and attached, but not the main structure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adjunctus, past participle of adjungere, to join to.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an extra vowel, as AD-juh-nunkt; the ending is one syllable.
Using adjunct as a synonym for associate professor, which is a different, usually tenured rank.

adjunct.etymology: From Latin *adiunctus*, perfect passive participle of *adiungō* (“join to”), from *ad* + *iungō* (“join”).

senses.definition: The act or practice of admitting.
senses.example: The museum's admission of new members is limited to one hundred per year.

senses.definition: Permission to enter, or the entrance itself; admittance; entrance; access.
senses.example: I request admission for two adults.

senses.definition: The granting of an argument or position not fully proved; the act of acknowledging something asserted; acknowledgement; concession.
senses.example: His admission that the data had been mislabeled surprised everyone at the review meeting.

senses.definition: Acquiescence or concurrence in a statement made by another, and distinguishable from a confession in that an admission presupposes prior inquiry by another, but a confession may be made without such inquiry.
senses.example: Her admission that the statement was accurate, given without prior questioning, was noted by investigators.

senses.definition: A fact, point, or statement admitted; as, admission made out of court are received in evidence.
senses.example: The lawyer read the defendant's admission into the record before the jury.

senses.definition: The cost or fee associated with attendance or entry.
senses.example: There is no way he has seen that show, the admission is more than he makes in a week.

core.definition: Permission to enter a place or join an institution, such as a school or hospital; also the entrance itself.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MISH, and the ending -sion sounds like 'shun'. Don't pronounce the first syllable as 'ad' with a long a; it is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for entry or acceptance, and it can also mean acknowledging a fact, which is a neutral to slightly formal use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use admission most often for getting into a college, hospital, museum, or event, and they often ask about admission fees or admission requirements. In the sense of acknowledging a fact, it appears in writing and formal speech more than in casual talk. Saying admission for a concert ticket is natural, but a formal word like admittance is less common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Admission is the broader word for being accepted or allowed in, while admittance focuses on the physical right or act of entering a restricted place.
Admission is a neutral statement that something is true, whereas confession usually implies guilt or a private revelation.

examples.everyday: Admission to the science museum is free on the first Sunday of every month.
examples.professional: Please review the admission criteria for the data science certificate before you submit your application.
examples.analytical: The admission of a premise, however reluctant, can reshape the entire structure of an argument.

nuance.analogy: Think of admission as the front door of a building: it is the moment you are let in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin admissio, from admittere, to let in or send to.
common_mistakes: Saying admission for a permission to enter a private room, where admittance or access is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable as AD-mission instead of ud-MISH-un.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.
senses.example: Many adolescent boys struggle to balance schoolwork, friendships, and their growing independence.

senses.definition: A person who is in adolescence; someone who has reached puberty but is not yet an adult.

core.definition: A young person between childhood and adulthood, typically from about age 10 to 19, who is going through puberty.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LES, the second main syllable, and the first syllable has a secondary stress. The final -ent is reduced to uhnt, so don't pronounce it as a full ent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a respectful term in medicine, education, and everyday talk, though some people prefer teen or teenager in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adolescent in medical, psychological, school, and policy contexts, such as adolescent health or adolescent development. In casual conversation, Americans usually say teen or teenager, and calling someone an adolescent can sound clinical or slightly condescending when describing a friend. As an adjective, it describes behavior or stages, such as adolescent behavior.

distinctions.note: Teenager refers to ages 13 to 19 specifically, while adolescent is broader and includes the early puberty years and is more technical.
Juvenile is a legal or formal term for someone not yet an adult, while adolescent refers to a developmental stage.
Youth is a general word for young people, while adolescent names a specific developmental stage.

examples.everyday: My sister is a teenager now, so she's suddenly very private about her phone.
examples.professional: Our health app needs age-specific advice for adolescent users rather than default adult guidance.
examples.analytical: Developmental psychology treats adolescence as a distinct stage, neither childhood nor full adulthood.

nuance.analogy: Adolescence is like a bridge: you are no longer on the childhood side, but you have not yet reached the adult side.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adolescens, present participle of adolescere, to grow up.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a long e, as in a-do-LES-sent, instead of the stressed LES.
Using adolescent as a casual word for any young person; for friends or relatives, teen or teenager is more natural.

adolescent.etymology: First attested?1440, from Middle English *adolescent*, from Middle French *adolescent* or directly from Latin *adolescentem*, accusative form of *adolescens*, present participle of *adolesco* (“to become adult, grow up”), from *ad-* (“to”) + *alesco* (“to…

senses.definition: To worship.
To love with one's entire heart and soul; regard with deep respect and affection.
senses.example: It is obvious to everyone that Gerry adores Heather.

senses.definition: To be very fond of.

core.definition: To love someone very deeply, or to be extremely fond of something; in religious use, to worship God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DORE, and the final r is pronounced in American English. Do not drop the r or say it as 'uh-DOO'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and strongly affectionate. It is warmer and more emotional than like or love, and it can sound dramatic when used for small things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adore casually for people, pets, food and things they love, as in 'I adore your dog.' It is stronger than like and can sound exaggerated for mild preferences. For mild interest, say 'I really like' or 'I love.' In religious contexts, adore means worship, and Catholics use it for Eucharistic adoration.

distinctions.note: Love is the general word for family, friends and food; adore is stronger and more emotional, so 'I adore my grandmother' sounds warmer than 'I love my grandmother.'
Like signals mild approval, while adore signals intense affection, so saying you adore a coffee shop sounds enthusiastic rather than casual.
Worship is the standard English word for religious devotion; adore is used in devotional writing for the same act, but in everyday talk it means strong affection.

examples.everyday: Oh, I adore this coffee shop, and the owner always remembers my name.
examples.professional: Our whole team adores the new dashboard, so please keep that layout when you ship the update.
examples.analytical: A theologian might argue that a person cannot truly know God without adoring him in worship.

nuance.analogy: Adore is like love turned up to full volume: the same feeling, but stronger and more visible.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adorare, 'to pray to, worship', from ad- 'to' plus orare 'to pray'.
common_mistakes: Using adore for mild preferences, which sounds exaggerated; say 'I like' when your interest is small.
Dropping the final r or stressing the first syllable, as in AD-or.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the Greek word proskynéō, 'to bow down, do obeisance, worship', is the word behind English adore. Matthew 4:10 records Jesus telling Satan that one must worship the Lord God and serve him alone. John 4:23-24 says that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. The RSV usually renders proskynéō as worship rather than adore.

adore.etymology: From Middle English **adoren*, *aouren*, from Old French *adorer*, *aorer*, from Latin *adōrō* (“to pray to”), from *ad* (“to”) + *ōrō* (“to speak”).

senses.definition: Concerned with beauty, artistic effect, or appearance.
senses.example: It works well enough, but the shabby exterior offends his aesthetic sensibilities.

senses.definition: Beautiful or appealing to one's sense of beauty or art.
senses.example: The design of the lobby cannot be considered particularly aesthetic.

senses.definition: The study of art or beauty.
senses.example: Her graduate thesis examined the history of the aesthetic, tracing how philosophers defined beauty from Plato onward.

senses.definition: That which appeals to the senses.
senses.example: The clean lines and warm colors of the kitchen create an aesthetic that makes guests feel at home.

senses.definition: The set of artistic motifs defining a collection of things, especially works of art; more broadly, their aura or “vibe”.
senses.example: Her most recent works have this quirky, nonchalant aesthetic inspired by ’90s teen culture.

core.definition: Relating to beauty or to the look and style of something, especially how it is designed or how it appeals visually.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, THET, not the first. The ae is pronounced like eh, and the ending is -ik, not a long ick sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, describing visual appeal. It can sound pretentious when someone dismisses a thing as purely aesthetic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aesthetic in everyday talk about looks, as in the aesthetic of a room or a brand, and it is more natural than artistic in those cases. On social media, the aesthetic is a common noun for a mood or vibe. Saying something is purely aesthetic suggests it has no practical function.

distinctions.note: Artistic describes making or valuing art; aesthetic describes how something looks or feels in terms of beauty and style, which can apply to anything.
Decorative means added for ornament; aesthetic can refer to the overall visual character, including the design itself.

examples.everyday: I love the aesthetic of this coffee shop, with the exposed brick and plants everywhere.
examples.professional: We need to keep the app's aesthetic consistent with the brand guidelines, so the new screens should match the older ones.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that aesthetic judgment is disinterested, since we find an object beautiful without desiring to possess it.

nuance.analogy: Aesthetic is the outfit of a thing: it shows how it looks and feels, even if it does the same job underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aisthētikos, of perception, from aisthanesthai, to perceive.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AYS-thet-ik; the stress belongs on THET.
Using aesthetic as a synonym for artistic in every case; it often refers to appearance or visual style.

aesthetic.etymology: From German *Ästhetik* or French *esthétique*, both from New Latin *aesthēticus*, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek *αἰσθητικός* (“of sense perception”), from *αἰσθάνομαι* (“to feel”); analysable as *aesthesis* + *tic*.

core.definition: Name of two women in 1 and 2 Samuel: David's wife and mother of Amnon, and Saul's wife.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOH, the third syllable, which has a long O like 'go'. The final syllable is a reduced 'uhm', not a full 'ahm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a proper name, used when discussing the Bible and the history of David and Saul.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name in Bible study about David and Saul, in 1 and 2 Samuel. Because two women share it, say 'David's wife Ahinoam' or 'Saul's wife Ahinoam' to make clear who you mean.

distinctions.note: Abigail was also one of David's wives, from Carmel, a different woman in the same story; Ahinoam is the Jezreelite wife.

examples.everyday: My cousin's kids are reading about Ahinoam, David's wife, in their Bible story book.
examples.professional: In my course on 1 Samuel, I list the wives of David and Saul, including Ahinoam, so students can track the family relations.
examples.analytical: The narrator in 1 Samuel 25 and 27 uses Ahinoam of Jezreel as a marker of David's shifting alliances during his years in the wilderness.

nuance.analogy: Like a name shared by two people in one family, you have to add the relationship to tell them apart.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Ahinoam, probably meaning 'my brother is pleasant' or 'brother of pleasantness'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable and saying AH-hih-noh-um.
Naming one Ahinoam without saying whose wife she was, which leaves listeners confused.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Ahinoʿam' (אֲחִינֹעַם), probably 'my brother is pleasant'. Key passages: 1 Samuel 14:50 names Ahinoam as the daughter of Ahimaaz and the wife of Saul; 1 Samuel 25:43 says David took Ahinoam of Jezreel as a wife; 1 Samuel 27:3 notes that she went with David to Ziklag, along with Abigail; 2 Samuel 3:2 names her son Amnon as David's firstborn.

senses.definition: Of persons, of the same kin; related by blood.
senses.example: Her grandmother and I were akin, sharing the same great-grandfather.

senses.definition: Allied by nature; similar; partaking of the same properties; of the same kind. [ with to]
senses.example: Her frustration was akin to mine when the server crashed during the demo.

senses.definition: (rare) To relate or compare; to liken.
senses.example: I like to akin the P-Diddy case to Gen-Z's version of the O.J. Simpson trial.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Similar in nature or character; related in kind, even if not by family.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and reduce the first to a quick schwa, like the 'a' in 'about.' The final sound is short, rhyming with 'in' and 'pin.' Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use akin mostly in writing, speeches, and thoughtful conversation, usually with 'to.' It sounds slightly elevated, so in casual talk people more often say 'similar to' or 'like.' It can be used positively or negatively, depending on what is being compared.

distinctions.note: Similar is neutral and everyday, while akin suggests a deeper, more fundamental likeness of nature or spirit.
Related often means connected by family or a clear logical link, whereas akin describes a shared quality or feeling.

examples.everyday: The excitement I felt on the first day of vacation was akin to a child's joy.
examples.professional: Our new monitoring dashboard is akin to the old one, so the team should adapt quickly.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats love as akin to desire, yet he insists that its proper object is God.

nuance.analogy: Two things that are akin are like cousins in the same family of ideas: not identical, but clearly from the same line.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'akin,' from the phrase 'of kin,' meaning related by blood or family.
common_mistakes: Using 'akin with' instead of 'akin to,' which is the standard pattern.
Using akin for simple surface similarity, where 'similar' is more natural.
Mispronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, as in 'AY-kin.'

akin.etymology: From a corruption of *of kin*, from Middle English *of kyn* (“related, of kin”), equivalent to *a-* + *kin* (1550s).

senses.definition: Steadfastly loyal, especially to a monarch or government.
A person who is loyal to some (specified or implied) thing; one who is allegiant.
senses.example: The old general was the most loyal allegiant the crown had ever known.

core.definition: Faithfully loyal to a ruler, government, or cause, especially in a formal or public sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEE, and the final syllable is a reduced 'unt', not 'ant' as in insect. Keep the 'j' sound soft and short.

nuance.connotation: Positive, because it describes steadfast loyalty, though it can sound old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'allegiant' in speech; it appears mostly in writing, history, and formal descriptions of loyal supporters. In everyday talk, people say 'loyal' or 'faithful'. A natural everyday substitute is 'They stayed loyal to the mayor through everything.'

distinctions.note: 'Loyal' is everyday and broad, while 'allegiant' is more formal and suggests duty to a ruler, government, or formal authority.
'Faithful' often describes personal devotion, such as to a partner or friend, while 'allegiant' describes loyalty to an authority or cause.

examples.everyday: Our old mayor had a few allegiant supporters who showed up to every rally.
examples.professional: The regional managers remained allegiant to the CEO throughout the restructuring.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether officials who stayed allegiant to the crown during the rebellion acted from principle or self-interest.

nuance.analogy: Like a flag that stays fixed to its pole even in a strong storm.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from 'allegiance' with the adjective suffix '-ant'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'allegiant' with 'allergic', 'elegant', or 'allergen' because of similar sounds.
Using 'allegiant' in everyday conversation where 'loyal' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Followed by away: to treat (something) as allegorical or symbolic rather than as truth.
senses.example: Modern readers often allegory away the miracles so they seem less troubling.

senses.definition: Synonym of allegorize.
senses.example: Critics allegory the poem into a meditation on exile.

senses.definition: To interpret (a picture, story, or other form of communication) to reveal a hidden, broader message about real-world issues and occurrences.
senses.example: Students in the seminar allegory the prophets' visions as commentary on their own era.

senses.definition: To create an allegory (noun sense 2.1) from (a character, an event or situation, etc.); also, to use one or more symbols to depict (a hidden, broader message about real-world issues and occurrences).
senses.example: The playwright allegories the bureaucrat's rise as a cautionary tale about ambition.

senses.definition: To interpret an allegory.
senses.example: The class spent an hour trying to allegory Dante's dream sequence line by line.

senses.definition: To create or use allegory.
senses.example: Spenser was willing to allegory openly, weaving courtly virtues into every canto of his epic.

senses.definition: The use of symbols which may be interpreted to reveal a hidden, broader message, usually a moral or political one, about real-world issues and occurrences; also, the interpretation of such symbols.
senses.example: The painting's heavy use of allegory made its political message impossible to miss.

senses.definition: A picture, story, or other form of communication in which one or more characters, events, or places are used to reveal a hidden, broader message about real-world issues and occurrences.
senses.example: Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution and its aftermath.

senses.definition: A character or thing which symbolically represents someone or something else; an emblem, a symbol.
senses.example: In the play, Greed is an allegory for the banker who ruins the village.

senses.definition: A category that retains some of the structure of the category of binary relations between sets, representing a high-level generalization of that category.
senses.example: Freyd's allegory captures the algebra of relations between sets in a more abstract setting.

core.definition: A story, picture, or text in which characters and events symbolize a deeper moral, political, or spiritual meaning; also, interpreting a text this way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: AL-uh-gor-ee. The second syllable is reduced to 'uh,' and the 'g' is hard, as in 'go.' Don't say 'uh-LEG-uh-ree.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in biblical interpretation it can be positive or negative depending on the tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use allegory for stories like Animal Farm or Pilgrim's Progress. In Bible studies it also names a method of interpretation, sometimes viewed with suspicion by those favoring literal readings. The word is mainly a noun; the verb use in the dictionary senses is rare, and 'allegorize' is the normal verb.

distinctions.note: A metaphor is a single figure of speech, whereas an allegory is an extended story or text carrying a symbolic meaning throughout.
A parable is a short story illustrating a lesson, usually realistic; an allegory assigns a symbolic meaning to many individual elements.
A symbol is a single thing standing for an idea, while an allegory is a whole narrative built from symbols.
An analogy explains by comparison, while an allegory conveys meaning through a symbolic story.

examples.everyday: We read Animal Farm in high school, and I didn't realize it was an allegory until the teacher explained it.
examples.professional: The film is a thinly veiled allegory about corporate greed, which made it a good topic for our ethics workshop.
examples.analytical: Origen's allegory sought a deeper spiritual meaning beneath the letter of Scripture, a method later critics accused of detaching texts from history.

nuance.analogy: An allegory is a story with a second story hidden underneath it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek allēgoria, 'speaking otherwise,' from allos 'other' + agoreuein 'to speak publicly.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with stress on the second syllable.
Using 'allegory' as a verb in ordinary speech; use 'allegorize.'
Treating allegory and parable as identical.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb allēgoreō appears once in the New Testament, in Galatians 4:24, where Paul says the story of Hagar and Sarah is to be taken allegorically, representing two covenants. Jesus' explanation of the parable of the sower (Mark 4:13-20) assigns meanings to its parts. Many scholars also read the Song of Solomon allegorically, a long tradition in both Jewish and Christian interpretation.

senses.definition: To fill or cover with alluvium.

core.definition: To fill, cover or build up an area with alluvium, the sediment deposited by flowing water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO, and the final syllable rhymes with ate. The -ate ending is a clear ayt, and the first syllable is a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Alluviate is rare and used mainly in geology and hydrology. Americans describing the same process in everyday speech would say the river silts up a valley or leaves sediment over the land. It is seldom used outside technical or academic writing.

distinctions.note: Silt up is common and informal, while alluviate is technical and specifically refers to deposits from flowing water.
Alleviate means to relieve pain or a problem and is a different word; the similar spelling is a common source of confusion.

examples.everyday: My uncle, a retired geologist, likes to explain how rivers slowly alluviate their valleys over centuries.
examples.professional: The model predicts the reservoir will alluviate within twenty years, which changes our dam maintenance schedule.
examples.analytical: Over geological time, the river will alluviate the lowland, burying older rock beneath successive layers of silt.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow tide leaving sand behind on a beach, one layer at a time, until the lower ground is buried.
nuance.etymology: From alluvium plus -ate.
common_mistakes: Confusing alluviate with alleviate, which means to relieve.
Stressing the last syllable (uh-LOO-vee-AYT) instead of the first heavy stress on LOO.

senses.definition: In reciprocal succession; succeeding by turns; in alternate order.
senses.example: Driving downtown is restricted to bikes with odd and even license plate numbers alternately by day of the month.

senses.definition: By alternation; when, in a proportion, the antecedent term is compared with antecedent, and consequent.
senses.example: In the proportion, the antecedents are compared alternately with the consequents.

senses.definition: Alternatively.
senses.example: You can pay by card or, alternately, by bank transfer.

core.definition: In turns, one after the other, in a regular repeating order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: AWL-ter-nuht-lee. The middle part is reduced, so do not say a long ay sound; it is not al-ter-NATE-lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes a pattern and carries no emotional value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alternately in recipes, instructions, and descriptions of patterns: alternately add flour and milk, or alternately warm and cool. In conversation, people more often say 'take turns' or 'back and forth'. Do not use alternately to mean 'or else' or 'another option'; that meaning belongs to alternatively.

distinctions.note: Alternately means in turns, one after the other; alternatively means as another option.
Simultaneously means at the same time; alternately means in turn, not together.

examples.everyday: Mix the flour and the milk in, alternately, a little at a time so the batter stays smooth.
examples.professional: The deploy script alternately updates the primary and replica servers to avoid downtime.
examples.analytical: The poem alternately praises and mourns the dead, so its feelings never settle into a single tone.

nuance.analogy: Like a metronome swinging back and forth, each beat taking its turn.
nuance.etymology: From alternate, from Latin alternus, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using alternately to mean 'or else'; say alternatively or or instead.
Saying the middle syllable as a long ay sound.
Confusing it with simultaneously; alternately means one after another.

senses.definition: Synonym of amnesia.

core.definition: Not a standard English word. People sometimes use it as a short form of amnesia, but the correct word is amnesia.

pronunciation.tip: If you hear it, say it like 'am' in 'ham'. Because it is not a standard word, do not try to stress it; when you mean memory loss, say amnesia instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It has no established meaning in standard American English.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would not recognize 'amm' as a standard word for memory loss, so do not use it in writing or speech. If you see it in a text or note, it is probably a typo, a clipping, or slang. Use 'amnesia' for memory loss, and 'forgot' or 'forgetful' for everyday lapses.

distinctions.note: Amnesia is the standard medical and everyday term for memory loss, while amm is not a recognized English word.

examples.everyday: My grandfather has some amnesia, so he forgets names, but he remembers old songs.
examples.professional: The report says the patient's amnesia came from a head injury, not from a stroke.
examples.analytical: Philosophers debate whether a person with amnesia remains the same self across the memories that have been lost.

common_mistakes: Using 'amm' in formal writing where 'amnesia' is needed.
Pronouncing amm with a long vowel, as in AHM, instead of a short vowel like the one in ham.

senses.definition: To disturb or irritate, especially by continued or repeated acts; to bother with unpleasant deeds.
senses.example: Marc loved his sister, but when she annoyed him he wanted to switch her off.

senses.definition: A feeling of discomfort or vexation caused by what one dislikes.
senses.example: Much to her annoy, the printer jammed again just before the deadline.

senses.definition: That which causes such a feeling.
senses.example: Constant pop-up ads are a daily annoy for anyone trying to read online.

core.definition: To bother or irritate someone, especially by doing something repeatedly that they dislike.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NOY, which has the 'oy' sound of 'boy'. Do not stress the first syllable or turn the ending into 'nay'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a mild but real irritation, and context can make it lighter or stronger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use annoy in everyday talk about small irritations, such as noise, interruptions or slow service. 'It really annoys me' is a common way to say something bothers you. Saying 'you annoy me' is blunt and can sound rude, so 'that really bugs me' or 'that's annoying' is softer.

distinctions.note: Bother is milder and often used for small inconveniences, while annoy suggests a stronger, repeated irritation.
Irritate can describe physical irritation of skin or throat as well as emotional irritation, while annoy is mainly emotional.
Exasperate is much stronger and means to make someone deeply frustrated, while annoy is everyday and lighter.

examples.everyday: Those phone notifications really annoy me when I'm trying to focus.
examples.professional: Repeated meeting reschedules annoy the client, so let's lock the calendar this week.
examples.analytical: A mere annoyance differs from a moral offense, although both can disturb us in similar ways.

nuance.analogy: Like a pebble in your shoe, small but constant.
nuance.etymology: From Old French anoier, from Latin inodiare, 'to make odious', from in odio, 'in hatred'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am annoying' when you mean 'I am annoyed'. 'Annoying' describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Stressing the first syllable as AN-oy instead of uh-NOY.

annoy.etymology: From Middle English *anoyen*, from Old French *enoiier* (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin *inodio* (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin *odium* (“loathing, hatred”).

senses.definition: Required to justify one's actions (to somebody); accountable, responsible.
Able to be answered.
Correspondent, in accordance; comparable (to).
(rare) Of an argument: capable of being answered or refuted; admitting a satisfactory answer.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Required to justify your actions to someone, or accountable and responsible for something to another person or group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AN. The 'w' in 'answer' is silent, and the ending '-able' is a weak 'uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests obligation and can sound stiff in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'answerable to the board' or 'answerable to voters' in news and workplace talk. In everyday conversation, 'accountable' or 'responsible' is more common. A question that can be answered by data is also described as answerable, mainly in academic contexts.

distinctions.note: Accountable is more common in American workplace talk; answerable is slightly more formal and often takes 'to'.
Responsible focuses on being in charge of or causing something; answerable focuses on having to explain it to someone.

examples.everyday: I'm answerable to my landlord, so I can't throw a party in the apartment.
examples.professional: The project manager is answerable to the steering committee for every budget change.
examples.analytical: A decision is answerable to others only if the decider can give reasons that others can assess.

nuance.analogy: Like a pilot answerable to air traffic control: every move must be explained on request.
nuance.etymology: From answer plus -able, meaning able to be answered or called to account.
common_mistakes: Using answerable with 'of' instead of 'to' or 'for', as in 'answerable of the results' instead of 'answerable for the results'.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the 'w' in answer.

senses.definition: Relating to anthropology.

core.definition: Relating to anthropology, the study of human societies, cultures, languages and biological development, especially through fieldwork and comparison.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LAH, the second syllable of '-logical' is reduced, and the ending '-cal' is a light 'kuhl'. Keep the 'th' voiceless and the 'r' rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It usually sounds academic and technical, though it may also sound like a scholar's comment in ordinary conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in university courses, research reports, museums and journalism about cultures. In casual speech, people might say 'culture-related' or 'about how people live', but 'anthropological' is the normal technical word. Do not use 'anthropologic', which is rare and sounds unidiomatic.

distinctions.note: Anthropological concerns the study of humans, while anthropomorphic describes giving human traits to non-human things.
Sociological describes the study of social structures and groups, often in modern societies, while anthropological often involves cultures, fieldwork and long-term observation.

examples.everyday: She has an anthropological curiosity about why everyone at the diner orders the same thing every Friday.
examples.professional: Our product team used anthropological methods, like visiting customers at home, to understand how they really shop.
examples.analytical: A purely anthropological account of religion treats belief as a cultural system, while theology asks whether its claims are true.

nuance.analogy: An anthropological approach is like a careful visitor who watches a whole village before deciding what its customs mean.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'anthrōpos' (human being) and 'logos' (study), with the English suffix -ical.
common_mistakes: Using 'anthropologic' as a shorter form, which is uncommon in American English.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'an-thruh-PAH-luh-jick', which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: The study of humanity in its relation to the divine, as in Christian anthropology.
The scientific study of humans, systematically describing the ethnographic, linguistic, archaeological, and evolutionary dimensions of humanity using a holistic methodological framework.
senses.example: According to anthropology, there are six basic patterns of kinship terminology or kin naming systems.

core.definition: The study of human beings, their societies and cultures; in theology, the study of what a human being is in relation to God, including creation, sin and redemption.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on PAH, the fourth syllable from the end. The 'th' is voiceless /θ/, and the middle syllables reduce to schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday use it usually means the social science; in theology it means the doctrine of the human person.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans hear 'anthropology' as the study of human cultures and origins. Theologians specify 'theological' or 'Christian anthropology' to avoid confusion. It is a standard term in seminary and philosophy courses.

distinctions.note: Sociology studies societies and institutions, mostly modern ones, while anthropology studies human cultures broadly and comparatively.
Psychology studies the mind and behavior of individuals; anthropology studies humanity as a whole.
Theology is the study of God; theological anthropology is the part concerned with humanity before God.

examples.everyday: My daughter is majoring in anthropology because she loves learning how different cultures live.
examples.professional: Next week's seminar covers theological anthropology, especially how the church fathers understood the image of God.
examples.analytical: Every doctrine of salvation rests on an implicit anthropology: what a person is determines what a person needs.

nuance.analogy: If theology asks who God is, anthropology asks who we are in front of God.
nuance.etymology: From Greek anthropos, 'human being', + logia, 'study of'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; the stress is on -THRO-/PAH.
Pronouncing 'th' as 't' or 's'.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture has no single word for anthropology, but it addresses the subject: Genesis 1:26-27 says humans are made in God's image; Psalm 8:4-5 asks what is man that God cares for him; Romans 5:12-19 presents Adam and Christ as defining two ways of being human.

traditions.view: Humans are made in God's image with the aim of theosis, union with God. The fall brought mortality and corruption, but not inherited guilt.
Humans are body-soul unities made in God's image, wounded by original sin, but nature remains fundamentally good and is elevated by grace.
Protestants stress human sinfulness and the need for grace. Reformed thought often emphasizes total depravity, Lutherans the simul justus et peccator, and Arminians and Wesleyans prevenient grace.

anthropology.etymology: From New Latin *anthropologia*, from Ancient Greek *ἄνθρωπος* (“human, mankind”) + *-λογία*.

senses.definition: Having the property that, for any two distinct elements of S, at least one is not related to the other via R; equivalently, having the property that, for any x, y ∈ S, if both xRy and yRx then x=y.
senses.example: A relation R on set S is antisymmetric if xRy and yRx together imply x equals y.

senses.definition: Whose sign changes on the application of a matrix transpose or some generalization thereof:
senses.example: A bilinear form is antisymmetric when its sign flips under the matrix transpose operation.

senses.definition: Whose transpose equals its negative (i.e. M = −M);
senses.example: For a real matrix to be antisymmetric, its transpose must equal its negative.

senses.definition: That changes sign when any two indices are interchanged (e.g. Tijk = -Tjik);
senses.example: The Levi-Civita tensor is antisymmetric, since swapping any two of its indices flips the sign.

senses.definition: For which B(w,v) = -B(v,w).
senses.example: The bilinear form is antisymmetric, so B(w,v) equals negative B(v,w) for all vectors.

core.definition: Describing a relation where if x relates to y and y relates to x, then x and y must be the same element.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel in the middle syllables is a short, reduced sound, so do not say 'see' for each syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: You will hear this in discrete mathematics, order theory, and computer science courses, where teams talk about whether a relation is a partial order. Americans in everyday life never use it, so it belongs in technical discussions and proofs. Be careful not to confuse it with asymmetric, which is a stricter property.

distinctions.note: An asymmetric relation forbids xRx and also forbids mutual relation. An antisymmetric relation allows xRx but forbids two different elements relating to each other in both directions.
A symmetric relation requires that if xRy then yRx. Antisymmetry is a different condition that restricts mutual relation between distinct elements.

examples.everyday: My daughter's homework asked whether 'is a sibling of' is antisymmetric, and the answer is no, because two different people can be siblings of each other.
examples.professional: Before we deploy the ranking model, we need to check that the dependency graph's relation is antisymmetric so the topological sort is well defined.
examples.analytical: A relation on a set S is antisymmetric if for all x and y in S, xRy and yRx together imply x = y, which is the condition that makes a partial order possible.

nuance.analogy: It is like a one-way street between two different towns: you can't get from A to B and back to A unless A and B are the same place.
nuance.etymology: From anti- (against) plus symmetric, from Greek symmetria, 'proportion,' from sym- (together) plus metron (measure).
common_mistakes: Confusing antisymmetric with asymmetric, which forbids self-relation too.
Assuming antisymmetric means 'not symmetric'; it is a separate condition that can hold alongside symmetry in trivial cases.

senses.definition: To be or become aware of (something); to perceive.
senses.example: Standing in the dark kitchen, I apprehended a faint smell of smoke.

senses.definition: To acknowledge the existence of (something); to recognize.
senses.example: Few economists apprehended the risk of the housing bubble until it was too late.

senses.definition: To take hold of (something) with understanding; to conceive (something) in the mind; to become cognizant of; to understand.
senses.example: It took the team months to apprehend how the algorithm handled missing values.

senses.definition: To have a conception of (something); to consider, to regard.
senses.example: Many readers apprehend the novel as a parable rather than a straightforward history.

senses.definition: To anticipate (something, usually unpleasant); especially, to anticipate (something) with anxiety, dread, or fear; to dread, to fear.
senses.example: I apprehend the phone call from the hospital every time my father's test results are due.

senses.definition: To feel (something) emotionally.
senses.example: She could apprehend the grief in his voice, even though he said very little.

senses.definition: To learn (something).
