'Unfair' is the standard adjective for writing and serious talk; 'no fair' is a spoken exclamation.

examples.everyday: You got two turns and I only got one? No fair!
examples.professional: Wait, they got the extension and we didn't? No fair, we had the same deadline.
examples.analytical: Players call out 'no fair' when they sense that a rule was applied inconsistently, which shows an intuitive grasp of fairness.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee's whistle blown by the player who lost the call.
nuance.etymology: 'Fair' comes from Old English fæger, meaning beautiful or pleasing; the sense of just developed later.
common_mistakes: Using 'no fair' in formal writing, where 'unfair' is needed
Confusing it with 'no fear' by pronouncing the vowel as 'ee' instead of the 'air' sound

senses.definition: Characterized by a pledge to make no inquiries concerning the motives, circumstances, or identity of the person receiving an agreed benefit or performing a proposed action.
senses.example: The pawnbroker offered cash for any item, no questions asked, and never recorded names.

senses.definition: Without inquiring into the motives, circumstances, or identity of the person receiving a benefit or performing a proposed action.
senses.example: You do what I've told you to, no questions asked.

core.definition: Without asking for explanations, reasons, or details about the person or the situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ASK, and the -tions in 'questions' sounds like 'chunz', with the word ending in a soft z. Do not pronounce the 'ed' in asked as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means a generous policy; negative when it implies suspicious or shady dealings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for store return policies, lost-and-found services, or rescue help. It can imply that a service will not judge you. In a crime context it can suggest that no one is checking where something came from, so the tone depends on the situation.

distinctions.note: No strings attached means no conditions are required; no questions asked means no explanation is required.
Without asking is more neutral; no questions asked emphasizes that no inquiry will be made.

examples.everyday: The store takes returns within thirty days, no questions asked.
examples.professional: Our customer policy allows a full refund within thirty days, no questions asked.
examples.analytical: A policy of no questions asked may build trust, yet it also removes the information that would reveal fraud.

nuance.analogy: Like a vending machine that gives you a snack without wanting to know why you pressed the button.
common_mistakes: Using it as a question, as if the phrase itself asked something; it is an adverbial phrase.
Using 'no questions' without 'asked' in the standard phrase.

conversation.text: You can return anything within ninety days, no questions asked.
They took the broken toaster back, no questions asked.
I love this store because returns are no questions asked.

senses.definition: A peer; an aristocrat; ranks range from baron to king to emperor.
senses.example: The nobleman hosted a lavish banquet at his estate outside Vienna.

core.definition: A man of high social rank, such as a count, duke, or earl, usually with a hereditary title.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a light 'bul' with a syllabic l, and the final syllable is reduced to 'muhn.' Don't pronounce it as three full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is mainly used for historical or literary descriptions of titled men.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nobleman' for a man of noble rank in historical or literary settings. In modern speech they often say 'aristocrat' or 'member of the nobility,' and for Bible contexts 'nobleman' refers to a man of high birth or official rank.

distinctions.note: 'Aristocrat' is a broader term for anyone of the upper class, while 'nobleman' specifically refers to a man with a noble title.

examples.everyday: The old novel we read in class is about a young nobleman who falls in love with a farmer's daughter.
examples.professional: The museum exhibit describes a nobleman who funded the cathedral's restoration.
examples.analytical: In Luke's parable, the nobleman's journey to a far country exposes the expectations placed on his servants.

nuance.analogy: Like a title on a family crest: a man recognized by birth and rank, not by daily work.
nuance.etymology: From 'noble' (Latin nobilis) plus 'man,' a compound from Middle English.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'ble' instead of a light syllabic l.
Using 'nobleman' for a woman; 'noblewoman' is the correct term.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, the Greek word eugenēs, 'of good birth,' appears in Luke 19:12, where a man of high birth goes to a far country to receive a kingdom. The parable of the pounds (Luke 19:11-27) uses this figure to teach faithful service while the master is away. The nobleman's return and his judgment of his servants form the parable's main lesson.

senses.definition: Written works intended to give facts, or true accounts of real things and events. Often used attributively.
senses.example: Encyclopedias, how-to manuals and biographies are all considered nonfiction and so are kept in the nonfiction section.

core.definition: Books, articles and other writing based on facts and real events, rather than invented stories.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FIK, the second syllable. Say 'non' like 'John,' and pronounce '-tion' as 'shun,' not 'tee-on.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a category of writing without judgment about quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans sort bookstores and libraries into fiction and nonfiction, so the word is very common. It can be a noun ('I read nonfiction') or an attributive adjective ('a nonfiction book'). Common nonfiction types include history, biography, memoir and science writing. Americans usually write it as one word.

distinctions.note: 'Fiction' is invented narrative, while 'nonfiction' is based on real facts and events.
A 'memoir' is a type of nonfiction focused on the author's own life, while 'nonfiction' is the broader category.
'Factual' describes whether specific statements are accurate, while 'nonfiction' describes the kind of writing as a whole.

examples.everyday: I'm reading a nonfiction book about the history of coffee, and it's more interesting than I expected.
examples.professional: Our editor wants the nonfiction title ready for the spring list, with every citation checked.
examples.analytical: Creative nonfiction blurs the line between literary craft and factual reporting, raising questions about how much a writer may shape a true narrative.

nuance.analogy: Like a map of a real city, as opposed to a city invented for a video game.
nuance.etymology: From non- ('not') plus fiction, from Latin fictio, 'shaping, invention.'
common_mistakes: Writing it with a hyphen in American contexts, where 'nonfiction' is the standard form.
Stressing NON instead of FIK.
Using 'nonfiction' as a verb or confusing it with 'nonfictional' in noun positions.

senses.definition: Unequaled, unrivaled; unique.
senses.example: Her nonpareil storytelling made every sermon she gave feel fresh and personal.

senses.definition: A person or thing that has no equal; a paragon.
The blue underwing or Clifden nonpareil (Catocala fraxini), a species of moth distributed across the Palearctic; also any of a number of moths of other species.
senses.example: Collectors prize the blue underwing nonpareil, a moth whose hindwings flash bright blue in flight.

senses.definition: A painted bunting (Passerina ciris), a brightly-colored finch native to North America.
senses.example: From the porch we spotted a painted nonpareil perched on the thistle near the fence.

senses.definition: A small, flat chocolate drop covered with such pellets of sugar, similar to a comfit.
senses.example: She placed a dish of chocolate nonpareils on the table for the children's birthday party.

senses.definition: A caper (“pickled edible flower bud”) of the smallest size.
senses.example: Add a spoonful of nonpareil capers to the sauce for a sharper, briny finish.

senses.definition: (dated) A small pellet of white or colored sugar used as decoration on baked goods and candy.
senses.example: The old cookbook calls for a sprinkle of colored nonpareils on top of the frosted cupcakes.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) A size of type between ruby and emerald (or, in the United States, between agate and minion), standardized as 6-point; a slug of this size.
senses.example: The printer set the caption in nonpareil so it would fit under each small photograph.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person or thing with no equal; an unmatched example of excellence, a paragon.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable 'rel', which rhymes with 'bell'. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, and the r is clearly pronounced. Learners often stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonpareil in literary, formal or elegant writing to praise someone or something as having no equal. It is rarely used in casual speech, and in a toast or tribute it would sound refined. In everyday conversation people usually say one of a kind or second to none.

distinctions.note: Paragon is the more common American word for a model of excellence; nonpareil is more literary and suggests someone with no rival at all.
An exemplar is a typical model to imitate; a nonpareil is unmatched, so the emphasis is on uniqueness rather than on being a model.

examples.everyday: At the wedding toast, my uncle called my aunt a nonpareil cook, and everyone agreed.
examples.professional: Our lead engineer is a nonpareil when it comes to debugging distributed systems.
examples.analytical: The author is widely regarded as a nonpareil of nineteenth-century American prose, whose sentences resist any imitation.

nuance.analogy: If an ordinary team has many players who can be swapped, a nonpareil is the one player no one else on the field can match.
nuance.etymology: From Old French non pareil, not equal, from Latin non (not) plus par (equal).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, which sounds unnatural.
Using it as a plural 'nonpareils' with the meaning of many equals; it is typically singular in the sense of a unique person or thing.

senses.definition: A measure of how well an observed distribution approximates a normal distribution.
The state of being normal or usual; normalcy.
senses.example: Jessie was going to wear pants to school, but her brother persuaded her to wear shorts to preserve normality.

senses.definition: The concentration of a solution expressed in gram equivalent weights of solute per liter of solution.

core.definition: The state of being normal or typical; a return to how things usually are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable MAL, with a light 'nor' before it and a reduced 'uh' after. Avoid stressing the last syllable, as in 'nor-muh-LI-tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a state without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say normalcy for the state of being normal, as in 'a return to normalcy.' Normality is more common in technical contexts such as statistics and chemistry, and in British English. Using it in casual talk can sound slightly stiff.

distinctions.note: Normalcy is the everyday American word for being normal; normality is more technical or formal.
Normality is the state of being typical; normalization is the process of making something normal or standard.

examples.everyday: Once the kids were back in school, we finally felt a sense of normality again.
examples.professional: The analysts tested the residuals for normality before choosing the regression model.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have debated whether normality is a moral ideal or merely a statistical average.

nuance.analogy: Normality is the flat middle of a bell curve, where most cases cluster.
nuance.etymology: From normal plus -ity; normal from Latin normalis, from norma, 'rule.'
common_mistakes: Using normality in casual American speech where normalcy is the common word.
Putting the main stress on the last syllable instead of MAL.

senses.definition: There is nothing truly novel in existence; every new idea has some sort of precedent or echo from the past.

core.definition: Nothing truly new exists; every new idea or event has an earlier precedent or echo from the past.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stresses fall on 'NUTH' in 'nothing', 'UN' in 'under', and 'SUN'. 'Under the' reduces to 'UN-der thuh', and 'nothing' ends with an '-ing' sound, not '-ink'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound wise and consoling, or slightly dismissive, depending on the tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this proverb when someone presents an idea as brand new but it resembles something old, like a trend that returns. It is common in conversation and writing, and it sounds a bit reflective. Do not use it literally for something that really is new; a natural reply is 'True, history repeats itself.'

distinctions.note: 'History repeats itself' focuses on patterns in events, while 'nothing new under the sun' focuses on the idea that novelty itself is an illusion.
'Old hat' means familiar and outdated, usually with a dismissive tone, while 'nothing new under the sun' is a broader observation about all human ideas.

collocations: there's nothing new under the sun
nothing new under the sun, really
it's nothing new under the sun
the old saying nothing new under the sun

examples.everyday: Another diet with no sugar and no carbs? Well, there's nothing new under the sun.
examples.professional: The team presented the pricing model as innovative, but it's nothing new under the sun; we tested the same tiers in 2015.
examples.analytical: Qoheleth's claim that nothing is new under the sun presupposes a cyclical view of time that most modern thinkers do not share.

nuance.analogy: Like a remixed song: the beat sounds different, but the melody has been played before.
nuance.etymology: Taken from the Bible, Ecclesiastes 1:9 in the RSV, and reflecting the Hebrew phrase 'under the sun.'
common_mistakes: Using it for something that is genuinely new, which sounds sarcastic.
Saying 'nothing new in the sun' or 'under the sky'; the phrase is fixed.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from Ecclesiastes 1:9-10 in the RSV, where the Teacher, called Qoheleth in Hebrew, argues that what has been will be again and that the sun rises and sets in endless cycles. The Hebrew 'tahat hashamesh' means 'under the sun' and describes the earthly, human realm of experience. Ecclesiastes 1:14 uses 'hebel,' meaning breath or vapor, to describe life's fleeting and puzzling character; in 1:14, the Teacher says that all deeds done under the sun are vanity and a striving after wind.

nothing-new-under-the-sun.variant_of: there is nothing new under the sun

senses.definition: The act of notifying.
senses.example: The notification of the family took place the morning after the accident.

senses.definition: A specific piece of information that serves to notify.
senses.example: My phone's notification said the server backup had failed overnight.

senses.definition: A message, alert, or signal displayed by a system or application to inform the user of an event, update, new message, etc.
senses.example: A notification popped up on my computer.

core.definition: A message or alert telling you that something has happened, changed or needs your attention.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the 'kay' syllable, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. The last syllable is often a syllabic n with no vowel, so say 'shun' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be helpful or annoying depending on how often and how urgent the alerts are.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'notification' for phone and computer alerts, as in 'push notifications' or 'turn off notifications'. In formal settings it means a written or official notice, such as a notification of a rate change from a bank. In casual speech Americans often shorten it to 'notifs' or simply 'alerts'.

distinctions.note: A 'notice' is usually a formal announcement on paper or a sign, while a 'notification' is often an electronic alert or formal message.
'Alert' suggests urgency or danger, whereas 'notification' is more neutral and can be routine.

examples.everyday: I turned off my phone notifications so the buzzing wouldn't keep me up at night.
examples.professional: The app sends a push notification whenever a payment fails, so the support team can respond quickly.
examples.analytical: The statute requires written notification to every affected party before the contract can be terminated.

nuance.analogy: Like a doorbell: it tells you someone needs your attention, but it does not tell you what they want.
nuance.etymology: From Latin notificare, 'to make known', from notus, 'known', plus facere, 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables carelessly, as in 'noh-tih-FI-ca-tion', instead of the reduced vowels.
Using 'notification' as a verb; the verb is 'notify'.

notification.etymology: From Middle French *notification*, from Old French *notificacion*, from Latin *nōtificātiō*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to wedding and marriage.
Capable, or characteristic, of breeding.
senses.example: Nuptial displays in the male stickleback turn his belly bright red during spawning season.

core.definition: Relating to a wedding or marriage, such as a nuptial mass, nuptial vows, or nuptial ceremony.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ti' is pronounced like 'sh', and the final syllable is a reduced 'uhl'. Do not add an extra vowel between 'p' and 'sh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nuptial' mainly in formal writing, wedding announcements, or literary descriptions. In everyday speech, people say 'wedding' or 'marriage'. The adjective 'nuptials' as a noun is also used, usually in a formal or humorous way.

distinctions.note: 'Matrimonial' is also formal, but it is more often used for legal or institutional matters such as matrimonial law, while 'nuptial' is more common in describing the ceremony itself.

examples.everyday: The invitation said the nuptial ceremony would start at four, so we planned to leave early.
examples.professional: Our wedding planner confirmed the nuptial schedule with the venue and the caterers.
examples.analytical: In the poem, the nuptial imagery links the poet's love to the ideal of lasting marriage.

nuance.analogy: 'Nuptial' is the formal dress version of 'wedding': the same event, but in a more elegant outfit.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nuptialis, from nuptiae 'marriage, wedding', from nubere 'to marry'.
common_mistakes: Using 'nuptial' in casual speech where 'wedding' is more natural.
Mispronouncing it with a long vowel in the first syllable, as in 'NOOP-shul'.

nuptial.etymology: Latin *nūptiālis* (“pertaining to marriage”), from *nūptiae* (“wedding”), from *nūbō* (“to marry, to take as husband”).

senses.definition: That provides nourishment; nurturing.
senses.example: The nurturant environment of the small church helped new families feel at home.

senses.definition: That which nurtures; a nurturing factor or influence.
senses.example: Stable housing is a nurturant that many families in our town lack.

core.definition: Providing care, encouragement, and emotional support that helps a person or thing grow and develop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ture' ending sounds like 'chur,' and the last syllable is weak, so say 'unt' quickly rather than 'ant.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes warm, supportive care, often in psychology or parenting research.
nuance.usage_note: 'Nurturant' appears mainly in psychology, sociology, and academic writing, especially about parenting or caregiving behavior. Everyday Americans usually say 'nurturing' instead. The noun sense 'that which nurtures' is rare and mostly found in dictionaries. In casual conversation, 'She's very nurturing' sounds more natural than 'She's very nurturant.'

distinctions.note: 'Nurturing' is the everyday word, while 'nurturant' is more technical and common in research writing.
'Supportive' describes helping someone in general, while 'nurturant' focuses on caring for growth and emotional development.

examples.everyday: Her grandmother was so nurturant that every visit felt like a warm kitchen full of good food.
examples.professional: The manager's nurturant style helped new hires feel confident enough to ask questions in team meetings.
examples.analytical: Researchers distinguish nurturant parenting, which emphasizes warmth and responsiveness, from parenting that relies mainly on control.

nuance.analogy: A nurturant environment is like sunlight and water for a plant, supplying what growth requires.
nuance.etymology: From nurture plus the adjective suffix -ant, from Latin nutrire 'to nourish.'
common_mistakes: Using 'nurturant' in casual speech where 'nurturing' is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'nur-TOO-rant.'

senses.definition: Committed.
senses.example: I feel obligated to finish the project I promised my team.

senses.definition: Having an obligation; obliged.
Simple past and past participle of obligate.

core.definition: Feeling morally, legally or socially bound to do something; having an obligation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AH. The middle syllable is reduced to 'bluh', and the final -ed is a short 'id', not a separate 'ated'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it can suggest reluctant duty rather than free choice.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in American speech, especially in 'I feel obligated' or 'I'm not obligated to'. It means you feel you have to do something, sometimes against your wishes. It sounds a little heavier than 'I should'. In business and law, 'contractually obligated' is standard American usage.

distinctions.note: Obliged is more polite and can mean grateful, as in 'I'm obliged to you'; obligated is more about duty or a commitment.
Required describes an external rule; obligated describes a duty that a person feels or is under.

examples.everyday: I know you're busy, so please don't feel obligated to come to the party.
examples.professional: We are contractually obligated to deliver the audit report by Friday, so the timeline is fixed.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that a rational agent is obligated by reason itself, not by fear of punishment or desire for reward.

nuance.analogy: Being obligated is like a rope tied to your wrist: it pulls you in a direction whether or not you wanted to go.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obligatus, past participle of obligare, to bind, from ob- to plus ligare, to bind.
common_mistakes: Using 'obligated for' instead of 'obligated to' before a verb
Saying 'obligated payment' instead of 'obligated to pay'
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on AH

senses.definition: The quality of being oblique in direction, deviating from the horizontal or vertical; or the angle created by such a deviation.
Mental or moral deviation or perversity; immorality.
senses.example: The novel's narrator revels in obliquity, cheating friends and lying without remorse.

senses.definition: The quality of being obscure, oftentimes willfully, sometimes as an exercise in euphemism.
Axial tilt.

core.definition: The angle at which something tilts away from a straight line or plane, such as the tilt of Earth's axis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BLIK, the second syllable. The qu is pronounced kw, and the final -ity is a short 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; in its older moral sense it is negative and literary.
nuance.usage_note: In American English obliquity is used mainly in astronomy (the obliquity of the ecliptic) and geometry. Americans rarely use the moral sense today and would say perversity or depravity instead. For a simple tilt, most people say tilt or angle.

distinctions.note: Inclination is the general or technical word for a slope or tilt; obliquity often names the specific angle between an axis and a reference plane.
Obliqueness is the general quality of being slanted; obliquity is the measured angle or the technical term in astronomy.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked why we have seasons, and I said it's because of Earth's tilt, which astronomers call its obliquity.
examples.professional: The obliquity of the planet's axis changes the amount of solar energy our climate model has to account for.
examples.analytical: Some moralists treated obliquity of conduct as a sign of a disordered will rather than a single mistake.

nuance.analogy: Like a spinning top that leans slightly off upright, the planet's obliquity is the lean that produces the seasons.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obliquitas, from obliquus, slanting.
common_mistakes: Confusing obliquity, the measured angle, with obliqueness, the general quality
Stressing the last syllable (uh-blik-WIH-tee)

obliquity.etymology: From Middle French *obliquité*, from Latin *oblīquitās*, from *oblīquus* (“oblique”).

senses.definition: A person who occupies an office or a position.
senses.example: I cannot say the same of the current occupant of the position

senses.definition: A person who occupies a place.
A person sitting in a car or other vehicle.
The owner or tenant of a property.
senses.example: The fire marshal confirmed that every occupant of the apartment building had evacuated safely.

core.definition: A person who lives in, uses, or is inside a place such as a building, room, or vehicle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the middle syllables quickly and lightly. Do not pronounce a long 'oo' sound in the middle, and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise word that is often used in safety, legal, and transportation contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use occupant most often in safety and legal language, such as 'all occupants must wear seat belts' or 'the building occupants were evacuated.' In casual conversation people say 'the people inside,' 'the driver and passengers,' or 'the residents.' It is not rude, but it sounds slightly official.

distinctions.note: A resident lives somewhere on a regular basis, while an occupant may simply be present or using a space.
Occupier is a British legal term, while Americans normally use occupant for a person who uses a space.

examples.everyday: The sole occupant of the car was a teenager who was listening to music and waiting for her friend.
examples.professional: Building occupants must leave by the nearest exit when the fire alarm sounds, and then wait at the assembly point.
examples.analytical: The authority of an office is not identical with the occupant who holds it at any given time.

nuance.analogy: An occupant is like a guest who is actually sitting in the seat, not the person who designed the room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occupans, the present participle of occupare, 'to take possession of.'
common_mistakes: Using occupant to mean a job holder; say 'the person in the position' or 'the holder of the office' instead.
Confusing occupant with occupation, which means a job or an activity.

occupant.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *occupant* (present participle of *occuper*) or Latin *occupāns*, *occupantis* (present participle of *occupō*).

senses.definition: A poetic stanza consisting of eight lines; usually used as one part of a sonnet.
senses.example: The octave of the sonnet presents the problem, and the sestet offers the resolution.

senses.definition: The eighth defensive position, with the sword hand held at waist height, and the tip of the sword out straight at knee level.
senses.example: The fencer held his blade in octave, guarding the high line against his opponent's lunge.

senses.definition: The day that is one week after a feast day in the Latin rite of the Catholic Church.
senses.example: The parish will celebrate the octave of Easter with a special Mass next Sunday.

senses.definition: An eight-day period beginning on a feast day in the Latin rite of the Catholic Church.
senses.example: During the octave of Christmas, our choir sang carols at the cathedral every evening.

senses.definition: A small cask of wine, one eighth of a pipe.
senses.example: The merchant stored an octave of red wine in the cellar for the winter.

senses.definition: Any of a number of coherent-noise functions of differing frequency that are added together to form Perlin noise.
senses.example: In the terrain generator, each octave adds finer detail to the Perlin noise pattern.

senses.definition: The subjective vibration of a planet.
senses.example: Some mystics describe the planet's octave as a subtle vibration felt in the soul.

senses.definition: An interval of twelve semitones spanning eight degrees of the diatonic scale, representing a doubling or halving in pitch frequency.
senses.example: The melody jumps up an octave at the beginning, then later drops back down an octave.

senses.definition: The pitch an octave higher than a given pitch.
senses.example: The bass starts on a low E, and the tenor comes in on the octave.

senses.definition: A coupler on an organ which allows the organist to sound the note an octave above the note of the key pressed (cf sub-octave)
senses.example: The organist engaged the octave coupler to double the melody an octave higher.

core.definition: In music, the interval between two notes where the higher one has twice the frequency of the lower, spanning eight notes of a scale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHK. The final -ave is pronounced 'iv,' like 'give,' not 'ave' as in 'wave,' and it has no separate final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard music term and is also used in everyday talk about pitch and singing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use octave most often in music, for pianos, singing ranges, and instruments, as in 'play it an octave higher.' It appears in poetry as the first eight lines of a sonnet and in Catholic liturgy for the week after a feast, but those senses are rare in everyday speech. In casual conversation, you can say 'one octave up' or 'one octave down' for a note.

distinctions.note: Interval is the general term for the distance between two pitches, while octave names one specific interval of eight scale steps.
An octet is a group of eight performers or things, while an octave is a musical interval between pitches.
A sestet is the six-line second part of a sonnet, while the octave is the eight-line first part.

examples.everyday: Can you sing that part an octave lower? My voice can't reach the high notes.
examples.professional: The synth's sub-bass sits an octave below the lead line, so the mix needs a filter to keep it from muddying the low end.
examples.analytical: Two pitches an octave apart are heard as the same pitch class, a perception that organizes most Western scales.

nuance.analogy: Like the same person standing on a higher step: the same identity, at a different height.
nuance.etymology: From Latin octavus, 'eighth,' from octo (eight).
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as oc-TAVE instead of AHK-tiv.
Using octave for any group of eight; for a group of eight musicians or things, Americans say octet.

senses.definition: The property of being offhand.
senses.example: Your offhandedness is completely inappropriate in such an important situation.

core.definition: The quality of being casual or careless in manner or speech, often seeming uninterested or dismissive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAN. The -ed-ness ending is quiet: say 'duhd' and 'nuss' with reduced vowels, without a full 'ed' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral: it describes a careless or dismissive quality of manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation; they would say 'he was so casual about it' or 'his attitude was dismissive.' It appears mainly in writing, reviews, or analysis of tone. To describe a person's manner in speech, 'nonchalance' or 'casualness' is often clearer.

distinctions.note: Casualness describes a relaxed manner; offhandedness suggests the speaker is careless or uninterested in the topic.
Nonchalance is calm, unbothered indifference that can be admired; offhandedness is more often a fault of tone.

examples.everyday: It bugged me that he said it with such offhandedness, like it didn't matter at all.
examples.professional: The reviewer criticized the report's offhandedness about sample size, which made the results seem less credible.
examples.analytical: Beneath the offhandedness of the essay's tone lies a serious argument about how moral claims are made in ordinary speech.

nuance.analogy: Like a shrug in words: the gesture is quick and light, but it can dismiss what someone cared about.
nuance.etymology: From offhand plus the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of being.
common_mistakes: Confusing offhandedness, the quality, with offhandedly, the manner of an action.
Dropping the final 'd' sound in speech; say 'duhd-nuss' with a clear d.

senses.definition: Spontaneously or extemporaneously; done as one goes, or during another activity.
senses.example: The software program has a table of values for some results, but calculates others on the fly.

senses.definition: On the move.
senses.example: We grabbed coffee on the fly and caught the train with seconds to spare.

senses.definition: While in the air, without having touched the ground.
senses.example: Jones caught the ball on the fly.

core.definition: Spontaneously or while doing something else, without planning in advance, and often making adjustments as you go.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FLY, which has a long i diphthong. 'The' reduces to 'thuh', so the phrase sounds like 'ahn-thuh-FLY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing skilled adaptation; negative if it suggests careless improvisation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in business, software, travel, cooking and everyday talk: 'We changed the route on the fly.' It is a common American idiom for improvising quickly. A natural reply is 'Nice work adapting like that.'

distinctions.note: 'Off the cuff' describes remarks made without preparation, usually speech, while 'on the fly' describes adjusting actions or plans as they happen.
'Ad hoc' means created for a specific purpose, often formal, while 'on the fly' is informal and emphasizes real-time adjustment.
'Improvised' is a general term for made up without preparation, while 'on the fly' stresses doing it during the activity.

examples.everyday: The GPS rerouted us on the fly when we hit traffic on the bridge.
examples.professional: We can adjust the pricing on the fly without redeploying the whole service.
examples.analytical: A jazz musician improvises on the fly, yet her choices are constrained by harmony, rhythm and the tradition she has learned.

nuance.analogy: Like a pilot adjusting course in midair as the winds change.
nuance.etymology: 'Fly' comes from Old English flēogan 'to fly'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on fly' without the article 'the'.
Saying 'on the flight' instead of 'on the fly', which changes the meaning.

senses.definition: A person who opens something.
senses.example: The grocery store's opener was a retired locksmith who arrived before dawn every day.

senses.definition: A device that opens something; specifically a tin-opener/can-opener, or a bottle opener.
An establishment that opens.
senses.example: The late-night openers in the mall include two restaurants and a clothing store.

senses.definition: The player who starts the betting.
senses.example: Sam was the opener, so he had to bet first with a pair of jacks.

senses.definition: Cards of sufficient value to enable a player to open the betting.
senses.example: Without a pair of jacks, my hand was not an opener, so I folded.

senses.definition: A person employed to separate sheets of hot metal that become stuck together.
senses.example: The foundry hired an opener to pry apart the sheets of hot steel that had fused.

senses.definition: The first act in a variety show or concert.
senses.example: The comedian was the opener, warming up the crowd before the headliner took the stage.

senses.definition: The first in a series of events, items etc. the first remark or sentence of a conversation.
senses.example: The opener of her speech was a joke that made the whole room laugh.

senses.definition: A period of time when it is legal to commercially fish.
senses.example: The Maine lobster opener starts the first Monday in June, so boats head out at dawn.

senses.definition: A batsman or bowler who normally plays in the first two positions of an innings.
senses.example: The team's opener scored a century before lunch on the first day of the test.

senses.definition: The first game played in a competition.
senses.example: The season opener against our rivals drew a sellout crowd to the stadium.

senses.definition: A opening goal.
A pitcher who specializes in getting the first outs of a game before being replaced, either by a long reliever or a pitcher who would normally start.
senses.example: The Giants used an opener in the first inning, then brought in a long reliever.

core.definition: A tool or device for opening something, such as a can opener or a bottle opener.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, OH. The middle syllable is a reduced 'puhn', and the final -er is a light, r-colored vowel that is not a full 'ur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use opener for a kitchen tool, as in can opener or bottle opener, and the compound is usually said in full. The word can also mean a person who opens something, or the first event in a series, such as the opener of a game. In casual talk, people often say the full compound rather than opener alone.

distinctions.note: Can opener is the specific tool for opening cans; opener alone is general and needs context.
A corkscrew removes a cork from a wine bottle, while a bottle opener removes a metal cap from a beer or soda bottle.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the can opener from the drawer so we can open the soup?
examples.professional: The opener of our demo should show the three metrics that matter most, so keep it short and concrete.
examples.analytical: An opener in a debate often sets the framing that everyone else must answer, which is why it carries such weight.

nuance.analogy: An opener is like a key for a sealed container: the tool does one job, and the job is making access possible.
nuance.etymology: From open and the agent suffix -er, meaning one who or that which opens.
common_mistakes: Saying can-opener without context when talking about something else; the shorter opener is general.
Stressing the second syllable, as in uh-PEN-er; the stress is on OH.

opener.etymology: From Middle English *oppinnare,opynnare*, from Old English *openere*, equivalent to *open* + *-er*.

senses.definition: One or more pairs of small low-powered binoculars for use by members of the audience at a theatrical performance.

core.definition: Small, low-powered binoculars used by theatergoers to see the stage more clearly from a distant seat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GLASS, and the -es ending is a reduced 'uhz', not 'ez'. The first word, opera, gets a lighter stress, as in 'AH-pruh' with the r pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, somewhat old-fashioned term that suggests a classic night at the theater.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'a pair of opera glasses' and use the plural even for one item. They are most often seen in older theaters and opera houses. In everyday speech, Americans may just say 'binoculars', but opera glasses are the specific term for small theater binoculars.

distinctions.note: Opera glasses are smaller and have lower magnification, designed for close, indoor seats rather than outdoor viewing.
A telescope is made for very distant objects and is far too large or narrow to use in a theater.

examples.everyday: I brought my grandmother's opera glasses so we could see the actors' faces from the balcony.
examples.professional: The venue doesn't allow cameras, but opera glasses are fine in the auditorium.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century theatergoers used opera glasses to turn the audience itself into a spectacle, since watching others became part of the evening.

nuance.analogy: Like a zoom lens for a stage, bringing the singers closer from a distant seat.
nuance.etymology: Named for use at the opera, from opera plus glasses.
common_mistakes: Saying 'opera glass' in the singular; Americans normally say 'a pair of opera glasses'.
Using opera glasses for outdoor viewing; Americans would say binoculars.

senses.definition: The larger part of an organism, composed of tissues that perform similar functions.
senses.example: bodily organs

senses.definition: A body of an organization dedicated to the performing of certain functions.
senses.example: The student council is an organ of the university that represents undergraduate interests.

senses.definition: A musical instrument that has multiple pipes which play when a key is pressed (the pipe organ), or an electronic instrument designed to replicate such.
senses.example: She practiced Bach on the church's pipe organ every Sunday morning before services.

senses.definition: An official magazine, newsletter, or similar publication of an organization.
senses.example: The union's monthly organ printed my letter about the new parking policy.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of organ pipe cactus.
A government organization; agency; authority.
senses.example: The state environmental organ issued a new permit for the riverside factory this week.

senses.definition: The penis.
senses.example: The urologist explained that the organ was examined for signs of infection during the routine checkup.

senses.definition: (historical) An Asian form of mitrailleuse.
senses.example: Historians note that the Qing army deployed an organ gun, a crude predecessor of the machine gun.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A large keyboard instrument that produces sound by forcing air through metal or wooden pipes, often played in churches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, OR, and say that vowel like the 'or' in 'for.' The second syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'un,' not 'gan' or 'ahn.' The r is rhotic and clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, descriptive word, with positive associations of church music and solemn worship.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'organ' most often means the pipe organ in a church, school or concert hall. Electronic versions, such as the Hammond organ used in jazz and rock, are also called organs. Americans use 'organ' for body parts (liver, heart) in medical and everyday talk too, but in music contexts it always means the instrument. Saying 'Who plays the organ on Sundays?' is a normal way to start a conversation about church.

distinctions.note: A piano sounds when hammers strike strings and then fades, while an organ sustains each note for as long as the key is held and air keeps flowing.
A synthesizer generates electronic sounds of many kinds, while an organ, even an electronic one, is specifically designed to imitate the sound of pipes or to produce it from pipes.

examples.everyday: My aunt plays the organ at our church every Sunday morning, and she's amazing at it.
examples.professional: The sound engineer said the new organ needs its pipes tuned before the Christmas concert.
examples.analytical: Calvinist churches long excluded instruments from worship, while Lutheran congregations embraced the organ, so the instrument became a marker of confessional identity.

nuance.analogy: A pipe organ is like a giant set of whistles, each pipe producing one note, all fed by a single bellows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin organum, from Greek organon, meaning tool or instrument.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong stress, such as or-GAN, instead of OR-gun.
Forgetting the article in American speech, saying 'She plays organ' instead of 'She plays the organ.'
Assuming all electronic keyboards are organs, when Americans usually call them keyboards or synthesizers unless they imitate organ sound.

traditions.view: Traditional Orthodox worship is sung without instruments, a cappella, so the organ is generally absent from Orthodox liturgy.
The pipe organ has long been regarded as the principal instrument for liturgy, though other instruments may be used when they suit the worship and the church's norms.

Practice varies. Lutheran and Anglican churches have long used the organ, while many Reformed and Baptist congregations historically excluded instruments and many contemporary churches now use bands or keyboards.

organ.etymology: From Middle English *organe*, from Old French *organe* and Old English *organ*, both from Latin *organum*, from Ancient Greek *ὄργανον* (“an instrument, implement, tool, also an organ of sense or apprehension, an organ of the body, also a musical…

senses.definition: Correctness of doctrine and belief in regard to any doctrinal (i.e. philosophical or theological) system.
Conformity to established and accepted beliefs (usually of religions).

core.definition: Correct belief or accepted doctrine in a religion, philosophy, or system of thought, or conformity to established views.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OR. The final syllable is see, with a clear long e, and the ah in dahk is the cot vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means sound belief, but negative when it suggests rigid conformity and resistance to new ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orthodoxy in religious discussion, academic debate, and politics. It is more formal than everyday words like the usual way of doing things. Saying a view is challenging orthodoxy usually signals a serious intellectual or religious disagreement.

distinctions.note: Orthodox is the adjective describing someone or something that follows accepted belief, while orthodoxy is the noun for that accepted belief itself.
Dogma is a specific belief declared as certain, while orthodoxy is the whole body of accepted belief.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the old ideas about farming are just orthodoxy that nobody has questioned.
examples.professional: Our data team is challenging the orthodoxy that more features always improve the model.
examples.analytical: Early church councils defended a doctrinal orthodoxy against views they judged heretical.

nuance.analogy: Orthodoxy is like the official rulebook of a game that everyone agrees to follow.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orthodoxia, from orthos right and doxa opinion.
common_mistakes: Using orthodoxy as if it were an adjective instead of orthodox.
Confusing orthodoxy with orthopedics or other words starting with ortho-.

senses.definition: A tuned electronic circuit used to generate a continuous output waveform.
An instrument for measuring rigidity by the torsional oscillations of a weighted wire.
A pattern that returns to its original state, in the same orientation and position, after a finite number of generations.

core.definition: An electronic circuit or device that produces a continuous, repeating signal, such as a waveform used in music or computing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AH. The final -or is weak and becomes a rhotic er. Don't confuse it with oscilloscope, which has a different stress and meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oscillator mainly in electronics, music technology, physics, and mathematics. A guitar pedal or synthesizer may contain one. In everyday talk, people would describe the effect, such as a buzzing tone, rather than name the part.

distinctions.note: An oscillator generates a signal, while an oscilloscope displays a signal on a screen so you can see it.
An amplifier increases the strength of a signal, while an oscillator creates a signal in the first place.

examples.everyday: My guitar pedal has a built-in oscillator that makes the fuzzy buzzing tone I like.
examples.professional: The board's clock oscillator drifted with temperature, so the timing errors appear after a few hours of operation.
examples.analytical: Mathematically, an oscillator is any system whose state repeats through a cycle, so its behavior can be described by periodic solutions.

nuance.analogy: An oscillator is like a metronome that keeps producing the same steady beat until it is switched off.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oscillare, meaning to swing, with the suffix -or for a device or agent.
common_mistakes: Confusing oscillator (a signal source) with oscilloscope (a display device for viewing signals).
Stressing the final syllable, as in uh-SIL-uh-ter, instead of the first syllable.

senses.definition: A world beyond death; an afterlife.
A world other than the everyday world.
senses.example: She wrote poems about a quiet otherworld where the dead still shared meals with the living.

senses.definition: A mythical abode of otherworldly beings.
senses.example: In the old legend, the hero crossed the sea to reach the otherworld of the fairy kings.

core.definition: A realm beyond the ordinary world, such as heaven, the afterlife, or a magical or mythical place inhabited by spirits.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, 'UH', and the second part, 'wurld', has a strong r-colored vowel. Pronounce the final 'd' clearly, and do not turn the vowel into a long 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mystical, often evoking wonder, mystery or spiritual hope, though it can sound dramatic in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'otherworld' mainly in fantasy writing, poetry, folklore and spiritual writing. In everyday speech people more often say 'the afterlife', 'heaven' or 'the next world'. It can also appear in discussions of myths, such as Celtic stories of a land beneath hills and lakes.

distinctions.note: Afterlife refers to life after death in general, while otherworld can also mean a magical or fantastical realm that exists alongside the ordinary world.
Underworld means a place below the earth, often of the dead, while otherworld is any realm beyond ordinary life.

examples.everyday: When my grandmother talked about her late husband, she sometimes said he was in the otherworld now.
examples.professional: The game designer built the otherworld as a separate map with its own rules and creatures.
examples.analytical: Celtic tradition pictures the otherworld as a space reached through hills and lakes, not as a distant heaven above the earth.

nuance.analogy: Like a second room behind a closed door, the otherworld exists just beyond the everyday world, but you cannot walk into it normally.
nuance.etymology: A compound of other, from Old English óðer, and world, from Old English weorold.
common_mistakes: Using 'otherworld' for a different country or planet in ordinary speech; the word normally refers to a spiritual or fantastical realm.
Pronouncing the first syllable with a long 'oh' sound, as in 'oh-ther-wurld'.

otherworld.etymology: From Middle English *othyr world,oþerr werelld,oþer world*, from Old English *ōþer weoruld*, equivalent to *other* + *world*.

senses.definition: To experience, go through, or undergo (something).
senses.example: The family had outgone years of poverty before the father found steady work.

senses.definition: To travel faster than (someone or something); to outstrip, to overtake.
senses.example: The new electric sedan can outgo the old gas models on the highway.

senses.definition: The act or process of going out; an instance of this; an outgoing.
senses.example: The outgo of the expedition party from camp began before dawn.

senses.definition: The means by which something flows or goes out; an outlet.
senses.example: The old chimney provided an outgo for smoke from the kitchen stove.

senses.definition: (rare) A (quantity of a) substance or thing that has flowed out; an outflow.
senses.example: A steady outgo of river water drained the flooded field overnight.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Money or expenses that go out, as opposed to income; spending.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, GO, so the word is 'owt-GOH'. The 'ow' is a diphthong and the final vowel is long, as in 'go'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise financial word, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use outgo today, except in older writing or in formal discussions of budgets, paired with income. In everyday speech people say expenses, spending or costs. The word's other senses, such as 'to outstrip' or 'to experience', are archaic and you will almost never hear them.

distinctions.note: Outgoing (adjective) means friendly and sociable, while outgo (noun) means money spent. The spelling is close, but the meaning is entirely different.
Expenses is the everyday word for money spent, while outgo is formal and somewhat old-fashioned.
Outflow is a broad word for anything flowing out, while outgo is specifically about spending money.

examples.everyday: We're trying to keep our monthly outgo under control now that the rent has gone up.
examples.professional: Please compare quarterly income with outgo before we approve the new hire, so we know what we can afford.
examples.analytical: A household whose outgo consistently exceeds its income must eventually borrow or cut back, and no moral argument can change that arithmetic.

nuance.analogy: Outgo is like the water that leaks from a bucket: whatever goes out is outgo.
nuance.etymology: From out and go, from Old English ūtgān (to go out).
common_mistakes: Confusing outgo (money spent) with outgoing (friendly), as in 'She has a lot of outgo' when you mean she is outgoing.
Using outgo in casual conversation, where expenses or spending sounds more natural.

outgo.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *outgon* (“to go out, depart, leave; to come out, emerge; to escape; to protrude; of a sword: to be drawn; to emanate from; to accompany”), from Old English *ūtgān* (“to go out”), **ūtgān* (“to go out”), equivalent…

senses.definition: The sudden outward flowing of a large amount of something.
senses.example: The outpouring of donations after the flood surprised even the relief workers.

core.definition: A large, sudden outflow of something, especially emotion, sympathy, or support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POUR, with a clear American r after the vowel. The ending -ing is short, not a long 'eeng', and the first syllable is secondary.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, as in an outpouring of love or sympathy; it can be negative for a flood of anger or complaints.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use outpouring most often in news and public statements, such as an outpouring of support for the family or an outpouring of grief. It is a warm, somewhat formal word, so in casual talk people might say so many people showed up. It is usually followed by of.

distinctions.note: Flood suggests overwhelming, uncontrolled volume; outpouring is more often emotional and organized, like a community response.
Surge is a sudden increase in numbers or force; outpouring stresses an outward flow, often of feelings or help.
Outburst is a sudden, loud emotional reaction, often negative; outpouring can be positive, like sympathy or support.

examples.everyday: After the storm, there was an incredible outpouring of help from people all over town.
examples.professional: The launch drew an outpouring of customer feedback, so we are reviewing every ticket this week.
examples.analytical: The public outpouring after the tragedy revealed how shared rituals sustain communal identity, a point that Durkheim would have recognized.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam breaking, with water rushing out all at once; here the flow is feelings or help.
nuance.etymology: From out plus pouring, from Old English powrian, to pour.
common_mistakes: Using outpouring for a single small event; it implies a large, sudden flow.
Using a preposition other than of, as in outpouring for support; say an outpouring of support.

senses.definition: To run faster than.
senses.example: Can a tiger outrun a lion?

senses.definition: To exceed or overextend.
senses.example: Their spending began to outrun their income within a single year.

senses.definition: In ski jumping, the flat or uphill area past the landing point, where the skier can slow down.
senses.example: After landing, she skied through the outrun and glided to a gentle stop.

senses.definition: The sheepdog's initial run towards the sheep, done in a curving motion so as not to startle them.
senses.example: The border collie's outrun swung wide so the sheep would not scatter.

core.definition: To run faster than someone or something, or to get ahead of it by running.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, RUN, because this verb is stressed on its second part. The first syllable is 'owt,' and the r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe speed in sports or animals, or a situation that gets ahead of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use outrun for racing or chasing, such as a dog outrunning a car or a runner outrunning a storm. It is common in sports and everyday speech. In business or planning, people may say a situation 'outran our control' to mean it moved faster than they could manage.

distinctions.note: Outrace is more explicitly about a competition, while outrun can describe escaping or getting ahead of something by running.
Escape means getting away from danger, while outrun specifically means being faster than someone or something chasing you.

examples.everyday: Our dog can outrun any squirrel in the park, but he never catches one.
examples.professional: Demand for the service quickly outran our capacity, so we had to add servers this month.
examples.analytical: Our theories sometimes outrun the evidence, which is why careful argument must be disciplined by observation.

nuance.analogy: To outrun something is like a swimmer pulling ahead of the current: you move faster than the force that is trying to keep up with you.
nuance.etymology: From out plus run, meaning to run beyond or faster than.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; the verb is stressed on RUN.
Confusing it with 'run out,' which means something is used up or exhausted.

senses.definition: Paddle a surfboard or kayak away from the shore.
senses.example: Before sunrise, we paddled out past the breakers to catch the first waves.

core.definition: To paddle a surfboard or kayak away from the shore, past the breaking waves, to reach the surfing area.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OUT, and the first word is reduced with a syllabic l. Link the words so they sound like pad-ul-OUT, not pad-ul and then out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Surfers in the United States use paddle out for leaving the beach to reach the waves. It is casual surf culture language. It can also describe a ceremony where surfers paddle out together to honor someone. A natural reply is 'Let's go' or 'See you out there.'

distinctions.note: Paddle back in means returning to shore; paddle out means heading away from shore.
Head out is general for leaving; paddle out specifically describes moving across water to the surf.

examples.everyday: Let's paddle out before the wind picks up.
examples.professional: Our surf club newsletter reminds members to paddle out in pairs for safety.
examples.analytical: To paddle out is to cross the breaking waves before one can ride them.

nuance.analogy: Like swimming out through a crowd at a doorway to reach the room where the action is.
nuance.etymology: From paddle, to move through water, and out, away from the shore.
common_mistakes: Using paddle out for a boat trip on a lake when surfers use it for reaching waves.
Placing the stress on paddle instead of out.

conversation.text: The surfers paddled out before sunrise.
It's hard to paddle out when the waves are this big.
Let's paddle out to the middle of the lake.

senses.definition: Speech or writing in which clauses or phrases are placed together without being separated by conjunctions.
senses.example: He said "I came; I saw; I conquered," is an instance of parataxis.

senses.definition: The juxtaposition of two images or fragments, usually starkly dissimilar, without a clear connection.
senses.example: The novel's parataxis with short scenes set side by side leaves the connections for readers to supply.

senses.definition: (historical) A coalition or "partisan camp" in the Ancient Greek political system.
senses.example: In the city's politics, the nobles formed a parataxis to block the reformers' laws.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A style of writing or speech that places clauses or phrases side by side without conjunctions such as 'and' or 'because'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -TAK-, the third syllable, with a short 'a' as in 'cat'. The final -is is a quick 'iss' sound, not 'eye-sis'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term in literary criticism and rhetoric.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parataxis mainly in literary criticism, rhetoric, and classics classes. Ordinary speakers would describe the effect as 'choppy' or 'short sentences.' It is a useful term when discussing style, but it sounds academic in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Hypotaxis links clauses with subordinating conjunctions that show dependence; parataxis links them as equals without such connectors.
Asyndeton is the omission of conjunctions in a list; parataxis is a broader style of placing clauses side by side.

examples.everyday: The short sentences in that novel feel choppy, almost like parataxis, one thought after another.
examples.professional: The report's bullet points read in parataxis, so the reader has to infer which finding causes which.
examples.analytical: Hemingway's prose relies on parataxis, placing short clauses beside one another to convey immediacy without explicit logical connection.

nuance.analogy: Parataxis is like a string of beads: each bead stands on its own next to the others, with no thread explicitly saying how they connect.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parataxis, a placing side by side, from paratassein, to place beside.
common_mistakes: Using parataxis as a synonym for paraphrase, which is a restatement in other words.
Mispronouncing the second-to-last syllable; the stress is on -TAK-.

parataxis.etymology: Ancient Greek *παράταξις* (“placement side by side”), from *παρα-* + *τάξις* (“arrangement”); equivalent to *para* + *taxis*.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name and clan name in the Old Testament, the ancestor of a family that returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a clear American r after the vowel. The final sh sound is a single hissing sound; do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name without everyday emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually encounter Parosh in Bible reading or study. It is a name rather than a word, so you would say the family of Parosh or the sons of Parosh. In conversation you would simply name the person or clan.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study, someone asked who Parosh was, and we found him in the list of returning families.
examples.professional: The seminar handout listed the clan of Parosh among the families in the postexilic census.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists in Ezra and Nehemiah name Parosh as the head of a clan whose members returned from Babylon and later joined the covenant renewal.

nuance.analogy: Parosh is like an entry in a family register: a name that marks a household and its place in a larger record.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Parosh, commonly glossed as flea, though the meaning of the name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in pa-ROSH.
Confusing Parosh with Paroch or other similar Old Testament names.
nuance.biblical_note: Parosh is the name of a family or clan head in the postexilic books of Ezra and Nehemiah, whose descendants returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and later took part in religious and civic life in Jerusalem. The Hebrew name is pārōsh. Ezra 2:3 lists the sons of Parosh among those who came back from exile, with a count of 2,172 in the RSV. Nehemiah 3:25 says that Pedaiah the son of Parosh repaired part of the wall near the Tower. Nehemiah 10:14 includes the leaders of the people, among them Parosh, who sealed the covenant to keep God's law.

senses.definition: Standard form of pay rise (“an increase in salary or wages”).
senses.example: After three strong years, Maria finally received a pay raise of six percent.

core.definition: An increase in the amount of money an employee is paid for their work, usually a higher salary or hourly wage.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun compound, the main stress falls on PAY, like 'pay phone', not on 'raise'. The final sound is a /z/, as in 'rays', so do not say 'rice'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; a pay raise is generally good news for the person receiving it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pay raise or simply raise for an increase in salary. British speakers often say pay rise, so avoid that form in American workplaces. People often say they got a raise, and a pay raise can also describe a general increase for many employees, such as one voted by a legislature. Give thanks when you receive one, for example 'Thanks, I really appreciate it.'

distinctions.note: Raise is the everyday American word for a salary increase; pay raise is slightly more explicit and common in formal or written contexts.
A bonus is a one-time payment, while a pay raise permanently increases your regular salary or wage.
A promotion changes your job title or responsibilities; a pay raise changes only the amount you are paid, though they often happen together.

examples.everyday: I finally got a pay raise, so dinner is on me this week.
examples.professional: Her manager approved a four percent pay raise after the annual performance review.
examples.analytical: Economists debate whether a broad pay raise can reduce turnover or simply feed inflation.

nuance.analogy: Like climbing one rung higher on a ladder: the same job, but a higher place on the pay scale.
nuance.etymology: Pay comes from Latin pacare; raise comes from Old Norse reisa, to lift up.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pay rise' in American workplaces; the usual American form is 'raise' or 'pay raise'.
Using raise as a verb with pay, as in 'They pay-raised me'; say 'They gave me a raise' or 'They raised my pay'.

senses.definition: A lever operated by one's foot that is used to control or power a machine or mechanism, such as a bicycle or piano.
senses.example: There are three pedals on manual cars, two on automatics.

senses.definition: A stirrup.
senses.example: The rider's foot slid out of the pedal as the horse bolted.

senses.definition: An orthopedic structure or a footlike part.
senses.example: The prosthetic's carbon pedal flexes with each step to mimic a natural ankle.

senses.definition: An effects unit, especially one designed to be activated by being stepped on.
senses.example: He stepped on the distortion pedal to add a gritty edge to the guitar solo.

senses.definition: The ranks of pipes played from the pedal-board of an organ.
senses.example: A small organ commonly has only one or two ranks on the pedal.

senses.definition: To operate a pedal attached to a wheel in a continuous circular motion.
senses.example: to pedal one's loom

senses.definition: To operate a bicycle.
senses.example: He was out of breath from pedaling up the steep hill.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the foot.
senses.example: The nurse checked the patient's pedal pulses after the vascular surgery.

core.definition: A lever worked by the foot to control or power a machine, such as the pedal of a bicycle or a piano.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second is a syllabic L with no full vowel, so say it as one unit. Pedal, peddle and the verb pedal are homophones, so spelling depends on meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical everyday term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pedal for the foot lever on bikes, cars and pianos, and most people think of a bicycle first. The verb means to ride a bike or work the pedals, so 'I pedaled to work' is a natural sentence. In cars, Americans casually say 'gas pedal' rather than 'accelerator'.

distinctions.note: Same pronunciation but a different meaning: peddle means to sell goods or spread something, not to push a lever with your foot.
A pedestal is a base that supports a statue or sink, while a pedal is worked by the foot.

examples.everyday: I was pedaling so hard up that hill I thought my legs would quit.
examples.professional: Our hardware team tested the pedal sensors on three electric bike models last quarter.
examples.analytical: The mechanism transfers force from the pedal to the chainring, so the pedal's leverage determines how much power the rider can deliver.

nuance.analogy: A pedal is a lever for your foot the way a steering wheel is a lever for your hands.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pedalis, 'of the foot', from pes, pedis, 'foot'.
common_mistakes: Confusing pedal with peddle: they sound identical, so choose the spelling by meaning.
Saying PAY-dul or PEE-dal; the first vowel is a short e, as in 'bed'.

pedal.etymology: French *pédale*, itself borrowed from Italian *pedale*, from Latin *pedālis*.

senses.definition: The state of being peevish.

core.definition: The quality of being irritable and easily annoyed over small things, often showing as complaining or sulking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ness is a reduced vowel, not a full 'ness' sound. Keep the middle 'ish' short, not 'eesh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a childish or sulky irritability, usually as a criticism of someone's mood or behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use peevishness to describe someone who is grumpy about minor things, such as a coworker who sighs at every request. It is more often said about a person's tone or mood than about a serious problem. In conversation, people more often say someone is being 'peevish' or 'cranky' rather than using the noun.

distinctions.note: Irritability is a general tendency to be easily annoyed and can be serious, while peevishness is milder and more childish, like sulking over a small slight.
Crankiness is more informal and conversational, often used for tiredness or hunger, while peevishness sounds more deliberate and slightly formal.

examples.everyday: I know you're tired, but your peevishness about the parking situation is getting old.
examples.professional: The peevishness in that email thread made the meeting harder than it needed to be.
examples.analytical: Her peevishness, a reaction more to small slights than to real injury, reveals a temperament that seeks out grievance.

nuance.analogy: Peevishness is like a small splinter of irritation that keeps poking at a conversation, never big enough to stop it but always there.
nuance.etymology: From peevish (adjective); the origin of peevish is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using peevishness for serious anger; it describes minor, childish irritation.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'pee-VISH-ness'; the stress is on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A pleasant smell; the scent, odor, or odoriferous particles emitted from a sweet-smelling substance; a pleasant odor.
senses.example: The bakery's perfume of cinnamon and warm butter drifted out onto the sidewalk.

senses.definition: A substance created to provide a pleasant smell or one which emits an agreeable odor.
senses.example: She bought a perfume at the airport.

senses.definition: To apply perfume to; to fill or impregnate with a perfume; to scent.
senses.example: She perfumed her letters with lavender oil before mailing them to her grandmother.

core.definition: A pleasant scent, or a liquid made to give a pleasant smell to the body or clothing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PUR. The second syllable 'fyoom' is like 'fume' with a 'y' sound, and the final syllable is not a long 'ME.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and pleasant, though some people find strong perfume unpleasant in shared spaces.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in stores, at home, and in conversation about gifts or fragrance. Many people now say 'fragrance' or 'cologne' for men, and in shops you will hear 'fragrance counter.' Be aware that some people are sensitive to strong scents, so mentioning fragrance-free products is also common in American offices and healthcare settings.

distinctions.note: Cologne is a lighter, less concentrated scent usually for men, while perfume is stronger and more concentrated.
Fragrance is a broader and more modern term used in stores and advertising, covering perfume, cologne, and other scented products.

examples.everyday: I bought my mom a bottle of perfume for her birthday, but she said it's too strong.
examples.professional: Please avoid wearing strong perfume in the office, since a coworker has a respiratory allergy.
examples.analytical: In the Song of Songs, the image of perfume evokes desire and the sensory delight of love.

nuance.analogy: Perfume is like an invisible signature: it announces your presence before anyone sees you.
nuance.etymology: From Italian per fumo, 'through smoke,' referring to incense burned to produce scent.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'per-FUME' with stress on the second syllable in everyday speech.
Using 'perfume' for body odor or a bad smell, which is the opposite of its meaning.
nuance.biblical_note: Perfume and fragrant ointment appear in Scripture as signs of honor, love, and worship; the Greek word myron (ointment, unguent) is often translated as perfume or ointment. Mark 14:3 describes a woman who breaks a flask of ointment of pure nard over Jesus's head at Bethany, and the act is praised. John 12:3 describes the house being filled with the fragrance of the same ointment, and Song of Songs 1:12 uses fragrance imagery to describe love.

senses.definition: The point, in an orbit about the Earth, that is closest to the Earth: the periapsis of an Earth orbiter.
The point, in an orbit about any planet, that is closest to the planet: the periapsis of any satellite.

core.definition: The point in an orbit where a satellite or the Moon is closest to the Earth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PER, with a clear r. The middle syllable is a weak uh, and the -ge is the j sound, so it rhymes with 'merry-jee' rather than 'per-i-GEE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise astronomical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perigee in astronomy, space news and weather or sky reports, especially when talking about a supermoon. For a planet's closest point to the Sun, Americans say perihelion instead. For a satellite's closest point to any planet, the more general term is periapsis.

distinctions.note: Apogee is the farthest point in an Earth orbit, the opposite of perigee.
Perihelion is the closest point in an orbit around the Sun, while perigee refers to an orbit around Earth or the Moon.

examples.everyday: The moon looks extra big tonight because it's near perigee, so it's a supermoon.
examples.professional: The satellite reaches perigee at about 400 kilometers, so we schedule the engine burn for that point.
examples.analytical: The orbit's eccentricity sets how far the perigee lies below the apogee, which determines how much atmospheric drag the spacecraft faces.

nuance.analogy: Like the tightest turn of an oval race track, where the car passes nearest the infield.
nuance.etymology: From Greek perigeion 'near the earth', from peri 'near, around' plus gē 'earth'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as per-IJ-ee. The main stress is on PER.
Confusing perigee with apogee, the farthest point, or with perihelion, the closest point to the Sun.

perigee.etymology: From French *périgée* via Latin *perigaeum*, ultimately from Ancient Greek *περί* (“near”) + *γῆ* (“Earth”).

senses.definition: The quality of being perishable.

core.definition: The quality of being likely to decay or spoil quickly, especially food or other goods.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves from PER-ish-uh-bul (perishable) to per-ish-uh-BIL-uh-tee. The t in -ty is often flapped to a soft d, as in ability, and many learners keep the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical property, most often of food, medicine, or goods.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in food safety, logistics, supply chain, and retail. In conversation they usually say goes bad quickly or spoils fast. Business reports often use phrases like high perishability, while perishable refers to the item itself.

distinctions.note: Perishables are the actual goods that spoil; perishability is the quality of being perishable.
Shelf life is how long a product stays good; perishability describes how easily it spoils.
Durability describes lasting under use or wear, while perishability describes decay over time.

examples.everyday: With fresh fish you have to think about perishability, so I buy it the same day I cook it.
examples.professional: We need to reduce the perishability of our dairy line, so I'm proposing a shorter route from the plant to the distributors.
examples.analytical: Her essay treats the perishability of data as an ethical problem, since models trained on outdated records quietly lose accuracy.

nuance.analogy: Perishability is like a carton of milk's internal clock: the product is fine until the clock runs out, and then it spoils fast.
nuance.etymology: From perishable, from Old French perissable, from perir 'to perish', from Latin perire 'to pass away'.
common_mistakes: Using perishability for the goods themselves; say perishables for the items and perishability for the quality.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable; the strongest stress falls on BIL.

senses.definition: The movement of a fluid through a porous or permeable solid.
The spreading of something (especially something malignant) through the body via blood vessels etc.
senses.example: Doctors feared permeation of the cancer into the lymph nodes and nearby blood vessels.

core.definition: The gradual passing or spreading of a fluid, gas or substance through a porous or permeable material or body.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on AY, the vowel of the -ate verb, while the first syllable has a lighter secondary stress. Be careful not to pronounce the -tion ending as 'tee-on'; it is the common 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. In medical contexts it can carry a negative sense, as when a disease spreads through tissue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use permeation in engineering, chemistry, medicine and environmental science, for example about gases passing through a seal or a drug crossing the skin.
